items.fullDescription: Anurag Kashyap, as an Indian film director, is to be identified as one who found himself in the crosshairs of transforming social-relations in post-liberalisation urban India and that of fast changing reception of Bollywood cinema in the wake of globalization. While Kashyap, incidentally, first tasted success in 1998, for the script to Ram Gopal Varma's 'Satya', it has to be noted that the trajectory of his acknowledgement as an auteur-director has neither been consistent nor the most traditional in the strictest sense of reception. Therefore, productions, such as 'Paanch' (2000), 'No Smoking' (2007), or even for that matter 'Gulaal' (2009) received very little attention, only to be declared to be of immense 'cult' value a decade or so later. His filmic oeuvre, often considered to be a part of 'Hat-Ke films' (Biswas, 2019), 'Non-Bollywood cinema' (M. Madhava Prasad, 2013), or even 'Mumbai Middlebrow" (Devasundram, 2016); wherein, the self-consciousness of being 'global' in terms of consumption of 'World Cinema' and producing 'Bollywood' films intertwine with each other, thereby creating a disruption to the narrative flow of films by interrogating the pre-Economic Liberalisation grand récit of nation, family and gender. This self-consciousness could be identified, as a possible reformulation of the binaries of 'Global' and 'Bollywood' to replace that of the 'national' and the 'modern'. With his involvement in the Anurag Kashyap Films (2005-present) and Phantom Studios (Formerly Phantom Films, 2010-2018), Anurag Kashyap began to be hailed as one of the sincerest and well-respected 'auteurs' of neoliberal Bollywood, wherein his films have not only remained a permanent fixture in foreign film festival circuits, and has promoted newer directors such as Vikramaditya Motwane, Bejoy Nambiar, Neeraj Ghaywan and debuts of 'bankable' actors such as Vicky Kaushal. Having been an outsider himself within the Bollywood social habitus, Kashyap's meteoric yet inconsistent rise from the margins to the centerfold of Bollywood, where in the global flows of corporate capital meet the self-conscious cinematic of the internationally respected auteur, augments the neoliberal mode of cinematic consumption and its marketability in the best possible way. The proposal for this volume has already been peer reviewed once by a publisher of international acclaim. Based on the recommendations of the same, we are presently, ONLY AND EXCLUSIVELY looking for papers on the following topics/films: · Anurag Kashyap's OTT productions (ex. Sacred Games, Nishaanchi, Bad Cop and other minor ventures. We are looking for atleast one dedicated contribution on Sacred Games) · "Paanch" (2003) · "Kennedy" (2023) · Gender Politics vis-à-vis formation of women characters/ feminine agency in his films. (excluding Gulaal and Gangs of Wasseypur, for which we already have enough contributions) · Global reception of Anurag Kashyap's filmography through film festival circuits and international circulation. PLEASE NOTE THAT WE ALREADY HAVE ENOUGH PAPERS ON GULAAL AND GANGS OF WASSEYPUR, LIKEWISE WE WOULD NOT BE ABLE TO ENTERNTAIN ANY NEW CONTRIBUTIONS ON THEM. We have as of yet garnered interest from an academic publisher on international repute. This cfp is thus in keeping with the initial peer review responses received on the proposal. This volume will be edited by Dr. Devapriya Sanyal (Assistant Professor, Department of English, St. Joseph's University) and Rajarshi Roy (Assistant Professor, Department of English, Vivekananda Satavarshiki Mahavidyalaya). Please email your proposals of around 250--300 words to ak1anthology@gmail.com by 30th October, 2026. Subsequent decision would be communicated on a rolling basis. Prospective contributors will be expected to submit their full chapters of (approximately) 6,000-7000 words including endnotes (referenced in Chicago style) by 15th November , 2026. Please note that while we encourage contributions from all social cultural dispensations, we are ideally looking for contributors who presently have completed and received their doctoral degrees. Devapriya Sanyal is Assistant Professor in School of Communication and media Studies, St. Joseph's University, Bangalore where she teaches film studies, and literature and researches on Film, Gender Studies, Urban Studies and Environmental Humanities. She is the author of several books on film and gender such as Failed Masculinities: The Men in Satyajit Ray's Films (Edinburgh University Press), Gendered Modernity and Indian Cinema: The Women in Satyajit Ray's Films (Routledge, UK), Salman Khan: The Man, The Actor, The Legend (Bloomsbury, India) and Through the Eyes of a Cinematographer: The Biography of Soumendu Roy(Harper Collins).Her latest books on post-independence Hindi film directors titled Bollywood and the First Decade of Independence: Seven Directors in Search of a Nation was published by Routledge UK in July 2025 and about the woman film director Aparna Sen titled Aparna Sen: A Life in Cinema was published by Rupa in August 2025. Her writings have appeared in national and international journals. She has degrees in English and Film Studies from Lady Brabourne College and JNU. Dr. Rajarshi Roy serves as an Assistant Professor at the Department of English, Vivekananda Satavarshiki Mahavidyalaya, Jhargram. He has been awarded a doctorate for his thesis titled 'The 'faithful' Republic and its representations in Indian literary and public discourses: A Study of the changing natures of secularism in post-Independence India', which is prersently under a monograph contract with Springer Nature. He is also one of the editors of the "Green Tagore" series under contract to be published from Peter Lang. He has in the past, been a recipient of the UGC-RUSA 2.0 fellowship to translate Prasanta Kumar Paul's 'Rabijibani' to English from Bangla. He also serves as an Editor (Consulting), Persons with Special Needs and Rehabilitation Management: Issues in Cultural Diversity and Wellbeing, Jadavpur University.

items.fullDescription: The Music Area in the Popular Culture Association invites submissions from individuals or organized panels (3 or preferably 4 persons) focusing on any topic relating to any genre of music. Topics can include but are not limited to individual artists, albums, CDs, genres, scenes, trends, periods, performances, critics, magazines, music and art, music on radio, television, and on stage and in academia. Abstracts on any topic of music will be considered. Please submit your abstract of approximately 150 words through the link provided on the Association's website: pcaaca.org. Submissions will only be accepted through the PCA website. Individuals must be current, paid members to submit to the conference. For panel submissions, panel chairs should include their abstract and title of their paper as well as the title of the panel, names of panelists, and a 50-word summary of the panel's focus. Individual panelists should submit their abstracts separately. Please specify any special scheduling needs at the time of submission. Feel free to contact the area chair with any questions: Eric Abbey, PhD Oakland Community College 739 S. Washington Ave Royal Oak, MI 48067 248-396-2649 ejabbey@oaklandcc.edu

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers (submission deadline October 31, 2026) Fairy Tales Area, American Popular Culture Association Annual Conference, 2027 Boston, MA, March 24-27, 2027 The Fairy Tales Area of the Popular Culture Association invites proposals for individual papers, panels, and roundtables for the 2027 annual conference in Boston, MA, March 24-27. We welcome submissions on all aspects of fairy tales, wonder tales, folk narratives, and their afterlives in literature, film, television, digital media, visual culture, performance, education, gaming, and popular culture more broadly. Papers may address oral tradition, literary fairy tales, folklore collections, adaptations, retellings, reception, translation, theory, pedagogy, gender, race, class, disability, nationalism, childhood, religion, ecology, material culture, or transnational circulation. For the 2027 conference, the Fairy Tales Area is especially interested in submissions related to two featured topics: 1. Adaptation of Fairy Tales This topic invites papers on fairy-tale adaptation across historical periods, genres, and media. Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: • contemporary retellings of fairy tales in fiction, film, television, theater, comics, games, and digital media; • fairy-tale villains, monsters, anti-heroines, and sympathetic retellings of traditionally negative figures; • identity, reflection, self-authorship, trauma, agency, and transformation in fairy-tale adaptation; • adaptation as cultural critique, remediation, commercialization, or popular mythology; • fairy-tale motifs across national, linguistic, and media boundaries. 2. Vladimir Propp's Historical Roots of the Wondertale. Marking the publication of the first English translation of Vladimir Propp's Historical Roots of the Wondertale (Indiana University Press, 2025), the Fairy Tales Area invites papers that revisit this major work and consider its continuing relevance for fairy-tale studies, folklore, narratology, adaptation studies, etc. Topics include but are not limited to: • Propp's Historical Roots of the Wondertale in relation to ritual, initiation, kinship, magic, social transformation, and other social and cultural contexts; • uses of Historical Roots of the Wondertale for analyzing particular tales, tale types, motifs, characters, spaces, objects, or narrative functions; • applications of Propp's work to contemporary fairy-tale retellings, fantasy, film, television, animation, gaming, digital storytelling, and other forms of popular culture; • the relevance of Historical Roots of the Wondertale for studying adaptation or recontextualization of older wonder-tale in modern media; • the place of national wonder tales in international fairy-tale scholarship, including issues of translation, circulation, reception, and comparison; • theoretical and methodological reassessments of Propp's work, including comparisons between Morphology of the Folktale and Historical Roots of the Wondertale, Propp's place in structuralism, narratology, folklore studies, anthropology, literary studies, and popular culture analysis, or the strengths and limitations of his method. Submissions on other fairy-tale topics are also welcome. Additional possible topics include: • Afanasiev, the Grimms, Perrault, Basile, Andersen, and other collectors or authors; • oral tradition and literary fairy tales; • fairy tales in film, television, animation, and streaming media; • fairy tales, gender, and sexuality; • fairy tales and religion, ritual, myth, or magic; • fairy tales and pedagogy; • fairy tales in translation; • fairy tales, horror, fantasy, and speculative fiction; • fairy-tale spaces, objects, bodies, animals, and transformations. Besides the scholarly analyses of fairy tales, we may consider creative and artistic projects that engage with fairy-tale traditions, themes, narratives, and their contemporary reinterpretations. Please submit an abstract of approximately 250 words by October 31, 2026. Panel proposals should include a title and brief description of the panel, along with abstracts and bios for each participant. Scholars at all career stages, including graduate and undergraduate students, independent scholars, and international scholars, are welcome. For questions about the Fairy Tales Area, please contact Dr. Olena Leipnik, Fairy Tales Area Chair, PCA, at soc_ovl@shsu.edu

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies Southwest Popular / American Culture Association (SWPACA) 48th Annual Conference, February 17-20, 2027 Marriott Albuquerque Albuquerque, New Mexico https://swpaca.org Proposal submission deadline: October 31, 2026 Proposals for papers and panels are now being accepted for the 48th annual SWPACA conference. One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. The Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies area invites paper proposals on topics related to Taylor Swift and/or Swifties from multiple vantage points. Since her debut in 2006, Taylor Swift has become a fixture of popular culture. Her career has been marked by incredible record-breaking highs and infamous tabloid-fodder lows. Known for her sharp lyrics, her evolving cross-genre musical styles, and her dedicated, creative fanbase (the Swifties), Swift's influence has been noted within music, fashion, economics, politics, and other cultural spheres of power. As an interdisciplinary area, we invite papers from multiple perspectives and disciplines. Topics might include, but are not limited to: • Critical interpretations of Swift's lyrics, eras, and/or personas • Considerations of Taylor Swift and politics, feminisms, activism and social justice • Interrogations of Swift and gender, race, class, and other identities/identifications • Analyses of Swift's connections to business, law, psychology, philosophy or other academic disciplines • Arguments about fandom, belonging, relating, creating and other Swiftie concerns • Examples of Taylor Swift's pedagogical relevancy All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Individual proposals for 15-minute papers must include an abstract of approximately 200-500 words and a brief summary of 100 words or less. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. SWPACA offers monetary awards for the best graduate student papers in a variety of categories. Submissions of accepted, full papers are due January 1, 2026. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Taylor Swift and Swiftie Studies area, please contact its Area Chair, Juliette Holder at jholder1@csustan.edu. If you have general questions about the conference, please contact us at support@swpaca.org, and a member of the executive team will get back to you. This will be a fully in-person conference. If you're looking for an online option to present your work, keep an eye out for details about the 2027 SWPACA Summer Salon, a completely virtual conference to take place in June 2027. We look forward to receiving your submissions!

One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. Esotericism, Occultism, and Magic invites proposals relating to magical worldviews, practices, and representations, as well as consciousness transformation, the preternatural, the paranormal, hidden meanings, the power of transmutation, and related phenomena. Characteristic methods, beliefs, perspectives, paradigms and techniques include: arcane symbolism, imagery, and aesthetics; unseen forces, spiritual intermediaries, invisible agencies, nonhuman intelligences; synchronous patterns, non-ordinary causation, and anomalous processes. Examples of ideas and systems include Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Sufism, Tantra, Rosicrucianism, Freemasonry, Satanism, witchcraft, sorcery, demonology, astrology, alchemy, yoga, shamanism, parapsychology, as well as psychic and paranormal phenomena, along with beliefs and practices relating to altered states of consciousness, overlapping with the study of mysticism and New Age spirituality, channeling, positive thinking, manifestation, reality shifting, the power of intention, numerology, guardian angels, and Ascended Masters. Esoteric, occult, and magical concepts, beliefs, and practices appear in every culture and civilization; contemporary media and popular culture have embraced them enthusiastically, yet at times have reacted against them. The impact of esotericism, occultism, and magic on genre formation/content and popular cultural perceptions has been profound. Their themes and tropes continue to become increasingly prevalent throughout all media of popular entertainment, including arts, music, literature, film, television, anime, comics and graphic novels, as well as being nearly ubiquitous throughout interactive gaming of all categories and genres. Beyond entertainment media, esoteric, occult, and magical concepts and content appear in online memes and frequently in fashion accessories and aesthetics. Their popularity continues to inspire and provoke a variety of conspiracisms in reaction, along with various fads, trends, moral panics, witch-hunts, witch-crazes, and conspiracy theories. Examples include demonic intelligences in "AI" chatbots, anti-occult-conspiracism in QAnon; adrenochrome confabulations, Illuminati paranoia, bloodline of the Holy Grail beliefs, Satanic Ritual Abuse scandals. All reactions to, and polemics against, esoteric, occult, and magical content in popular culture, as well as projections concerning its presence, are therefore also suitable topics for this Area, as are political, religious, secular, scientific, and scientistic receptions of esotericism, occultism, and magic, along with instrumentalization of related concepts, beliefs, and practices in propaganda, intelligence, and information warfare. All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Individual proposals for 15-minute papers must include an abstract of approximately 200-500 words and a brief summary of 100 words or less. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. SWPACA offers monetary awards for the best graduate student papers in a variety of categories. Submissions of accepted, full papers are due January 1, 2026. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Esotericism, Occultism, and Magic area, please contact its Area Chair, Dr. George J. Sieg, Luna Community College, georgejsieg@gmail.com . items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTERS The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature Editors: Mariusz Finkielsztein (University of Gdan?sk) mariusz.finkielsztein@gmail.com Josefa Ros Velasco (Complutense University of Madrid) josros@ucm.es The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature is to be a comprehensive monographic study examining boredom as a central aesthetic, philosophical, psychological, and socio-cultural category in the history of modern literature. Rather than relying purely on abstract theory, this volume approaches boredom through focused case studies devoted to individual authors and their works. Across these chapters, boredom-alongside adjacent states such as ennui, tedium, spleen, acedia, melancholy, existential malaise, and affective exhaustion-emerges variously as paralysis, protest, privilege, illness, and spiritual crisis. By situating close textual readings within the broader intellectual history of modernity, the volume, written by a multidisciplinary group of authors, is to demonstrate that literary boredom is a powerful diagnostic lens on social order, temporality, and the modern subject's experience of meaninglessness. Volume Structure & Epochal Scope The volume is planned as a Handbook or Companion and covers not only the most vital writers addressing the theme of boredom but also a broad selection of modern authors (around 60 chapters). The book is to trace the evolution of literary boredom across (tentatively) seven historical and thematic phases: Early Modernity & Enlightenment Foundations: Early reflections on existential void and social routine (e.g. Diderot, Laclos, Austen). Romantic Ennui (1770s-1840s): Melancholy, idealist frustration, and the world-weary anti-hero (e.g., Goethe, de Stae?l, Senancour, Byron, Chateaubriand, Constant, Stendhal, Sand, Balzac, Musset). The Superfluous Man: The Russian literary archetype of social paralysis, alienation, and unfulfilled potential (e.g. Pushkin, Lermontov, Goncharov, Turgenev). Bourgeois Boredom, Realism, & Decadent Spleen: Domestic stagnation, industrial monotony, social entrapment, and aesthetic decay (e.g., Dickens, Flaubert, Tolstoy, Fontane, Chopin, Ibsen, Gilman, Conrad, Chekhov, Baudelaire, Huysmans, Wilde). Modernist Stagnation (Early 20th C.): Temporal distortion, consciousness, alienation, and metaphysical paralysis (e.g., Proust, Joyce, Pessoa, Mann, Kafka, Woolf). Catastrophism & Existential Absurdity (Mid-20th C.): Totalitarian dread, the absurdity of existence, and postwar existential malaise (e.g., Broch, Platonov, Orwell, H. Miller, Gombrowicz, Sartre, Camus, Beckett, Buzzati, Gracq). Postwar Emptiness, Consumerism, & Digital Fatigue: Mass society, late-capitalist hyper-consumption, information overload, and contemporary affective exhaustion (e.g., Moravia, Perec, de Beauvoir, Ernaux, Bellow, Bernhard, Duras, DeLillo, Houellebecq, Ferrante, Rourke, Moshfegh). Chapter Guidelines & Scope Each chapter must offer an in-depth analysis of the theme of broadly understood boredom in the work of a single author (according to a formula: Boredom in...). The title should include the name and surname of a writer as a main part, and a freely formulated subtitle. Analytical Approach: Authors may focus on a single representative work but should analyse boredom across multiple texts of an author to demonstrate how boredom functions as a recurring motif in the author's oeuvre. Target Audience: Written primarily for readers seeking to deepen their understanding of boredom in a specific author's work (spoilers are permitted), while remaining accessible to a general literary audience. Comparative analysis with other writers should be kept to a minimum. Required Contextual Elements: o Biographical Context: Key details situating the writer within their epoch. Where applicable, personal engagement with boredom (e.g., excerpts from letters, diaries) may be included. o Socio-Cultural Context: Historical background necessary to understand the specific societal structures depicting boredom (e.g., aristocratic class dynamics, marital systems, late-capitalist work environments, author's country history and socio-cultural context). Submission guidelines: The abstract of the proposed chapter (between 250-500 words) along with a short bio (up to 150 words) and contact information should be sent to editors via e-mail before the end of October 2026. Contributors may propose up to two chapters. Each submission must include a brief statement detailing: (a) how the chosen author's work relates to boredom; and (b) what the contributor's expertise is on the writer. The minimum criteria for inclusion of a writer are: the author must address themes of boredom/ennui, possess at least some international recognition, and be available in English translation. Poetry is excluded. The comments and decisions on the proposed chapters will be provided before the end of December 2026. Then, the proposal for the book will be sent to prospective publishers (Routledge Handbook Series, The Oxford Handbooks, The Cambridge Companions or The Palgrave Handbooks). In case of a positive answer from a publisher, the authors will be asked to prepare the chapter, between 6,000 and 8,000 words including footnotes and references. Technical information will be provided after the publisher accepts the proposal and will depend on the publisher's style. In case of any doubts and/or questions, we encourage prospective authors to consult the editors directly. Prospective deadline for chapters: mid-2028

items.fullDescription: Neurodivergent Studies - Popular Culture Association 2027 "Neurodivergent just means a brain that diverges." - Kassiane Asasumasu, Radical Neurodivergence Speaking Neurodivergent Studies at the PCA offers a chance for scholars to have conversations about how neurodivergent approaches to popular culture, fandom, academia, and our own experiences can shape the way we approach the world. Neurodivergent Studies promotes a very open approach to the subject, following in the footsteps of Kassiane Asasumasu, who is credited with coining the term "neurodivergent." Kassiane specifically notes that neurodivergent "is not another damn tool of exclusion. It is specifically a tool of inclusion. If you don't want to be associated with Those People, then YOU are the one who needs another word. Neurodivergent is for all of us" (sherlocksflataffect). Following Asasamasu's leadership, Neurodivergent Studies invites papers on the following topics: o Neurodivergence in popular media o Neurodivergence and/or madness o Neurodivergence and/or disability o Neurodivergence and self/diagnosis o Neurodivergence and the social disability model o Neurodivergence and eugenics o Neurodivergence and intersectionality o Neurodivergence and race/racism o Neurodivergence and gender identity o Neuroqueer theory o Neurodivergent pedagogy o Neurodivergence in the academy o Neurodivergent activism o Neurodivergent community For the Boston 2027 conference, the PCA is running the theme "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." ND Studies provides a wealth of ways to approach this topic, including focuses on questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. Neurodivergent Studies welcomes paper proposals, roundtable proposals, or cross-listed panels with other PCA areas. Submissions are due October 31. We look forward to seeing you in Boston!

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Dime Novels and Juvenile Series Books, PCA 2027 The PCA Dime Novels and Juvenile Series Books Area is accepting proposals for presentations at the next PCA/ACA annual conference, to be held in Boston, MA from March 24-27, 2027. See the PCA website for more information on the conference and submission guidelines. The area has two distinct but related areas of interest: juvenile series books of all types and eras, including 20th-century publications like those of the Stratemeyer Syndicate and its imitators (Nancy Drew, Hardy Boys, Tom Swift, etc.), as well as more recent and ongoing series (Harry Potter, Twilight, Choose Your Own Adventure, etc.); and the series books' precursors: early popular publications for mass audiences of all ages (dime novels, nickel weeklies, story papers, etc.). Papers addressing either or both of these areas will be considered. Papers may cover (but are not limited to) any aspect of the following topics: authors, publishers, major characters, themes, readership, bibliography or research methods, social commentary, early or noteworthy genre forms, print culture, special collections, and representations of gender, race, class, sexuality, etc. Something new this year: the larger conference has a theme! The 2027 PCA conference theme is "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." Presenters in Dime Novels and Juvenile Series Books are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. However, area presenters might consider engaging with some of the following themes: Adaptations and retellings of dime novels (reboots of Nick Carter for radio and spy paperbacks; silent films and serials, like Frank Merriwell at Yale (1903), The Adventures of Frank Merriwell (1936), or Deadwood Dick (1940); film adaptations of Laura Jean Libbey stories, including A Poor Girl's Romance (1927), When Love Grows Cold (1925), and In a Moment of Temptation (1928); UPN's Legend series; and series fiction (e. g., the many book variations of Nancy Drew over the decades, the Hardy Boys/Nancy Drew Mysteries television show, the Tom Swift and Linda Craig Mystery Hour , the CW network shows of Nancy Drew and Tom Swift , the numerous film versions of Nancy Drew ). Revolutionary themes in any of the above - for example, are there dime novels that take place during the American or French Revolutions ( The Liberty Boys of '76 )? What is the purpose of setting the story in that time period? What do these dime novels and series books have to say about revolutions more generally, and revolutions in the time that they were published? Dime novels and series books that explore technological revolutions or feature the exploits of inventors, like Frank Read and Tom Swift. Fanfiction, transformative works, participatory culture, audience reception, and cultural memory. This could include series books that were based upon real people, such as the Annette Funicello Mysteries that were a five-book series, or the Janet Lennon books. It could include audience reception captured in film magazines or newspaper reviews. Participants do not need to be academics or professional writers; undergraduate submissions are welcome but require sponsorship by a faculty advisor, as per PCA policy. All participants are requested to submit a 250-word abstract with title. First-time participants with this division are encouraged to submit a 1-2 page proposal, including a bibliography, along with the abstract. Email communication is welcomed from potential members desiring feedback on a proposal topic prior to making a formal submission. Early submission is strongly encouraged. Submissions opened August 1, 2026 and are due by October 31, 2026. In order to submit an abstract, you must have an active PCA membership. Please send all inquiries to: Matt Short University of Northern Illinois mshort@niu.edu Emily Hamilton-Honey SUNY Canton emilyhamiltonhoney@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: John Steinbeck once remarked that fellow-Californian Robinson Jeffers wrote some the "greatest poetry since Whitman." Steinbeck kept a significant collection of Jeffers work both in his personal library and Ed Ricketts' Lab, where Jeffers was an influential topic in their endlessly varied conversations. When asked about possibility of meeting the poet, Steinbeck declined with a telling degree of reverence: "His poetry is perfect to me, and I don't think one should get the man mixed up with his work." Although they did eventually meet-notably when Steinbeck lived in Monterey in 1944-their relationship was one of distant, though friendly, mutual respect. Although these two writers rarely crossed physical paths, their work maintains a wide concurrence of concern. They both deeply engaged with Californian geography and history; they both emphasized the influence of the natural world upon the individual and society; they both had social circles that revolved around the Monterey Peninsula; they both were interested in psychoanalytical theory; they both were students of classical literature and philosophy; they both experienced extraordinary recognition at the peak of their literary fame (at one point, Jeffers was on the cover of Time magazine); they both were deeply uncomfortable with such a cultural spotlight; they both admonished personal humility in the face of environmental forces. Intersections such as these (and many more) deserve to be explored with more depth and significance. The editorial staff at the Steinbeck Review invites submissions for a special edition, "John Steinbeck and Robinson Jeffers." We are particularly interested in perspectives which put these authors into conversation in productive and even unexpected ways. Although submissions are not required to examine both authors, we strongly suggest that they engage (even if briefly) both Steinbeck and Jeffers. We welcome all critical and theoretical perspectives. Please see the full guide for submissions here and submit your paper to the Steinbeck Review's online submission system, found at www.editorialmanager.com/Steinbeck, no later than October 31, 2026. Decisions will be made by December 1, 2026. Submissions should be accompanied by an abstract and key words.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Siren! Magazine Second Issue: Disciplined Bodies, Transgressive Bodies, Transformed Bodies Link to the call: https://penn.manifoldapp.org/page/siren-current-call-for-proposals Bodies are shaped by the worlds we inhabit, the stories we tell about them, and the institutions through which we learn what a body is, what it should look like, how it should behave, and what it is permitted to become. Yet bodies are often treated as merely biological facts: fixed, self-evident, and prior to politics. This distinction matters because once something is understood as natural, the expectations attached to it can begin to appear inevitable. For this issue, we invite work on disciplined, transgressive, and transformed bodies. We are interested in work that reflects on how bodily norms are produced and enforced, what happens when bodies exceed or destabilize those norms, and how bodies are remade through political, social, technological, medical, aesthetic, and cultural processes. The question, then, is not only who tells bodies what to do, but how we come to understand what bodies are for in the first place and how we may challenge the constraints imposed over them. How do medicine, law, media, family, religion, workplaces, markets, states, and digital platforms make particular kinds of bodies appear normal, desirable, healthy, productive, legible, or valuable? What happens when a body does not fit the meaning assigned to it; when it refuses, cannot comply, fails to conform, or becomes something else? We are especially interested in moments when bodily categories begin to break down, when the meanings attached to bodies no longer hold, or become further reinforced and are resisted, and when bodies become sites of contradiction, refusal, negotiation, and possibility. Key terms For the purposes of this issue, we understand the three terms broadly and provisionally: Disciplined bodies are shaped by the norms, institutions, and expectations that surround them. They may be expected to reproduce, perform gender recognizably, be deemed healthy and desirable, remain productive and self-optimizing, regulate themselves, and stay intelligible to others. We welcome work on how these norms are produced, enforced, negotiated, and unevenly distributed. Transgressive bodies make those expectations difficult to sustain. Transgression need not be intentional: a body may refuse, fail, exceed, disrupt, or simply be unable to comply. Nor are particular bodies inherently transgressive; they are often rendered so by institutions and cultural frameworks that mark some forms of embodiment as abnormal, excessive, threatening, or unintelligible. Transformed bodies ask what happens when embodiments become a site of remaking. Bodies may be altered through medicine, technology, disability, transition, reproduction, labor, aging, artistic practice, environmental exposure, or political violence. Transformation may be desired or imposed, liberatory, or coercive. We are interested in what bodies become, what histories they carry, what forms of power shape them, and what futures they make imaginable. We welcome submissions that interpret one of these categories, bring two or more into conversation, question the distinctions between them, or propose other ways of thinking about bodily discipline, transgression, and transformation. Proposals should identify the term that most strongly connects to the submission while noting any significant intersections with the others. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: -Bodily autonomy and reproductive rights -Disability and debility -Gender and sexuality -Race and racialization -Beauty and aesthetic labor -Health, illness, and wellness -Medicine and biomedical technologies -Aging -Death -War and militarization -Sport and physical performance -Embodiment and mediation (digital or otherwise) -Surveillance -Cyborg subjectivities -Body modification -Bodily aesthetics -Migration and borders -Carcerality -Labor and productivity -Environmental harm -Colonialism and its afterlives -Speculative or imagined forms of embodiment Who can submit We welcome work from scholars, students, artists, activists, independent researchers, and public intellectuals working in communication, media studies, feminist studies, cultural studies, disability studies, queer and trans studies, critical race studies, the humanities, and related fields. Submissions are open to contributors at all career stages, but we particularly encourage work from early-career scholars and those whose work may sit outside conventional academic publishing structures. Formats Submissions may be written, visual, audiovisual, audio, or hybrid. We welcome experimental forms alongside conventional scholarly approaches. Across formats, submissions should engage the issue's broader commitments to critical feminist inquiry, transnational solidarity, feminist world-making, and transformative social change. Timeline For full consideration, abstracts are due by October 31, 2026, with decisions made by December 10th. Completed submissions will be due by February 10th, 2027, with a projected publication date in September 2027. Guidelines for proposal types -Paper: Please send the title and a 250-word abstract outlining the argument for a full paper featuring an original contribution. Full papers are long-form (3000-5000 words) analytical essays that connect to the current topic of the issue. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Escalator Paper: Please submit the title and a 150-word abstract for a short analytical piece (500-2000 words). Research escalator papers are works-in-progress on novel ideas related to the issue theme; they will be published as submitted and paired with an expert mentor to develop into a full analytical or empirical work. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Multimedia and Hybrid Submissions: Please submit the title and a 200-250-word description explaining how your piece relates to the current issue's theme. For multimedia works, explain how text and other elements interact. Finished pieces should include a link to a sample. For works in progress, add a brief (up to 100 words) outline of the concept, your process, and the timeline for completion. Experimental submissions are encouraged. Important dates Abstract due: October 31, 2026 Acceptances: December 10, 2026 Final submission: February 10, 2027 Peer-review process and mentorships: February - June 2027 Expected publication date: early September 2027 All proposals should be sent as a .docx or .pdf document, and include a brief bio (up to 150 words) introducing yourself and your background. Please submit proposals to asc-sirenmagazine@asc.upenn.edu, using the subject line "Siren Magazine - Bodies." Direct any questions regarding the call or submission process to the same address.

Call for papers | The Aesthetics of Mythmaking: Narrative, Culture, and Power "We are mythmaking creatures" (Ware 20...
items.fullDescription: Call for papers | Diffractions Issue 13 | The Aesthetics of Mythmaking: Narrative, Culture, and Power? Deadline for Abstracts: October 31st 2026 Deadline for Papers: January 31st 2027 Editors-in-Chief: Alyse Kaweng Fan, Thales Reis Alecrim? Call for papers | The Aesthetics of Mythmaking: Narrative, Culture, and Power "We are mythmaking creatures" (Ware 2025); human beings make and reinterpret myths. Mythmaking has remained a living action of the human cultural process since the earliest stage of human history. Myths are not static stories that stay unchanged across time; that is why agency and acts of mythmaking are powerful. Through mythmaking, inherited stories are continually adapted and reinterpreted to reflect changing cultural values and historical circumstances. Consequently, myth also assumes the form of a spectacle and ideology that must be critically examined; it often serves to naturalise or essentialise instances of domination, transforming contingent political agendas into "universal" truths. This call for papers values both the aesthetic brilliance of mythmaking in the arts and popular culture and the rigor critique of its ideological utility as a tool for hegemony. The inherent ambiguity of myth as both a meaning-making tool and a mechanism of control invites further scholarly exploration. We therefore seek to gather diverse perspectives on how these creative processes function across human experience, inviting interdisciplinary submissions that weave together multifaceted theories of myth and mythmaking.?? Even the same myth can be retold in radically different ways. For Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, the reinvented myth of Ozymandias represents a meditation on antiquity and the transience of glory. More than a century later, when Alan Moore rewrote Ozymandias in Watchmen, Shelley's ruined king was transformed into a morally ambiguous antagonist with the ambition to construct a new global saviour myth capable of uniting humanity. Moore's self-fashioned Ozymandias also evokes the myth of Superman, a figure that can be traced to Friedrich Nietzsche's concept (1883) of Übermensch (beyond-human). From Nietzschean philosophical ideal of self-overcoming, the Superman later takes forms in different myths: George Bernard Shaw's play and most famously in Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster's comics, where Superman represents the experiences and aspirations of Jewish immigrant communities before being incorporated into American national mythology during WWII and the Cold War. Superman mythmaking also transcended across the Pacific. In postwar Japan, superhumans like Astro-Boy and Ultraman reconstructed the archetype into social recovery and national renewal in the aftermath of atomic destruction. These examples show that mythmaking reinvents cultural symbols into new stories in response to political realities and collective memory. While myths are traditionally framed as archaic narratives of gods and heroes, modern scholars argue that the act of mythmaking can act as a mobilizing force in society and serves as a political power beyond its presence in art (Citton 2025; Josephson-Storm 2017). A political myth operates as a system of explanation, providing a cryptography through which the disconcerting chaos of contemporary facts is ordered and understood (Girardet 1987; Segal 2020). By offering an imaginary reading of a historical moment, myths restore intelligibility to a fractured world, manifesting in recurring structures like the nostalgia for a Golden Age or the yearning for a providential Saviour. However, this phenomenological reality of worldbuilding parallels Walter D. Mignolo's decolonial critique of "enunciation," where the content of myth is disseminated by the enunciator who ultimately possesses power (2018, 144-145).?? Mythmaking is still an ongoing cultural process without a singular definition. In a way, its study can be viewed as a consequence of the emergence of anthropology, which, during the 19th century, inquired about the concept of myth. This was the work of, for example, E.B. Tylor and J.G. Frazer. Yet, they were not so concerned about the aesthetics of mythmaking, as they viewed it as a form of "primitive knowledge" that was the exact opposite of Western art and science. Across the 20th century, authors as diverse as Bronislaw Malinowski (1922), Ernst Cassirer (1946), Claude Lévi-Strauss (1978), Northrop Frye (1967), Carl Jung (1964), Joseph Campbell (2004), and Mircea Eliade (1954) have suggested a whole range of different and often conflictive definitions for this concept. They actively engaged with the knowledge traditions of anthropology, philosophy, history, comparative literature, and religion studies.? One compelling form of analyzing mythmaking emerged at the intersection of aesthetics, philosophy, politics, and critical theory during the 19th century. Reacting against Enlightenment rationalism, German Romantics and Idealists such as Schiller, Schelling, and Hegel called for a "new mythology" to heal the alienation between humanity and nature while birthing the philosophical myth of absence-the belief that modernity is uniquely "mythless" (Josephson-Storm 2017, 17-21). This tension is central to the work of Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno, who, echoing Max Weber, argued that the Enlightenment's "disenchantment of the world" sought to dispel myths through reason, yet ultimately revealed that "enlightenment reverts to mythology" (2016, xviii), as instrumental rationality facilitated the domination of human beings over one another. In this way, inquiring the aesthetics of mythmaking involves a critique of different areas of the socio-cultural construct, reaching the realms of narrative, culture, and power.?? Amidst these diverse intellectual traditions and definitions of mythmaking, this call invites contributions that explore mythmaking as an ongoing process of cultural translation, forms of exercising power, political representation, and artistic (re)creation. We are interested in examining how mythmaking is still continually making, remaking, and mobilising new meanings and identities across historical periods, cultural contexts, and media forms. Proposals for thematic articles in response to this call are welcome, including but not limited to the following topics: ? Mythmaking and memory retelling? ? Superstition, hagiographies, and religion stories?? ? Mythmaking in different culturalforms: films, comics, and music? ? Mythmaking and Nationmaking?? ? Mythmaking as Tools of (De)colonial Discourse?? ? Mythmaking and Identity: theInvention of Tradition and Self-making? ? Mythmaking and Imaginary?? ? Lived experience and Phenomenology of Mythmaking ? The Power of Mythmaking in Social and Political Contexts? ? Mysticism and Poetry? ? Myth and Mythmaking in Literature from Romanticism to Modernism? ? Mythopoesia? ? Women Writers/Poets and Feminist Revisionist Mythmaking? ? The Role of Mythmaking in Visual Arts? ? The Study of Mythography in Modern Culture? ? Mythic ecology? ? Mythmaking, Philosophy, and Science: from myth to reason? ? Mythmaking and Psychology (Jungian Psychology, Psychoanalysis, etc)? Submissions and review process Abstracts will be received and reviewed by the Diffractions editorial board who will decide on the pertinence of proposals for the upcoming issue. After submission, we will get in touch with the authors of accepted abstracts in order to invite them to submit a full article. However, this does not imply that these papers will be automatically published. Rather, they will go through a peer-review process that will determine whether papers are publishable with minor or major changes, or they do not fulfil the criteria for publication.? Please send abstracts of 150 to 250 words, and 5-8 keywords by October 31, 2026, to info. diffractions@gmail.com with the subject "Diffractions 13", followed by your last name.? The full papers should be submitted by January 31, 2026, through the journal's platform, using our Style Sheet: https://revistas.ucp. pt/index.php/diffractions/ about/submissions.? Every issue of Diffractions has a thematic focus but also contains special sections for non-thematic articles. If you are interested in submitting an article that is not related to the topic of this issue, please consult the general guidelines available on the Diffractions website at https://revistas.ucp.pt/ index.php/diffractions/about/ submissions. The submission and review process for non-thematic articles is the same as for the general thematic issue. All research areas of the humanities are welcome, and we accept contributions in English or Portuguese.? References: Adorno, Theodor W., and Max Horkheimer. 2016. Dialectic of Enlightenment: Philosophical Fragments. Verso.? Bell, Michael. 2015. "Myth and Texts." In A History of Modernist Poetry, edited by Alex Davis and Lee. M. Jenkins. 46-67. Cambridge: Cambridge University?? Bell, Michael. 2016. "An Analytic Note on Myth in Modernism: The Case of T.S. Eliot." In Religion and Myth in T.S. Eliot's Poetry, edited by Scott Freer and Micahel Bell. 65-76. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing.? Campbell, Joseph. [1949] 2004. The Hero with a Thousand Faces. Princeton: Princeton University Press.? Cassirer, Ernst. 1946. Language and Myth. Harper & brothers.? Citton, Yves. 2025. Mythocracy: How Stories Shape Our Worlds. Verso Books.? Eliade, Mircea. 1954. items.fullDescription: THE SIXTIES Call for proposals: Papers, Sessions, Panels Popular Culture Association Annual Conference March 24-27, 2027 in Boston, MA The Sixties area of the Popular Culture Association welcomes submissions for papers and presentations on any aspect of popular culture from the era. Topics of interest might include, but are not limited to: Film, television, radio, and other media (underground press, posters, etc.) Analysis of influential books/authors, art/artists, films/filmmakers, etc. New developments in religion and spirituality Psychedelia and its many manifestations The sexual revolution Music and fashion, as cultural expression and/or consumer culture New social arrangements, e.g., communes, back to the land movement 1968 or other significant dates, places, or events, e.g., Freedom Summer, Days of Rage, etc. Countercultural movements, e.g., hippies, Diggers, SDS, Black Panther Party, White Panther Party, etc.Politics and protests of the era, e.g., Civil Rights, Vietnam War, Free Speech Movement, etc. Race and gender issues, e.g., Black Power, women's rights, etc. Media representations of/reactions to any of the above Rock music, the counterculture, or other developments in international/global contexts (i.e. outside the US and UK) The significance of the decade in contemporary society and culture, including ongoing debates and revised perspectives NOTE : This year PCA is trying out a wider shared theme for the conference, on the general subject of "Revolutions and Revisions in Popular Culture" - which obviously connects with many Sixties topics. As part of that theme, presenters are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, technological change, or changing cultural practices. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. ALSO : This year we are also featuring a joint panel between the Sixties area and the Radio, Podcast, and Sound Media area. items.title: Irony: Dramatic and Otherwise
items.location: University of Tübingen, Germany · Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate
items.excerpt: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it e...
items.fullDescription: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it evokes and reflects basic constituents of human communication: in particular, the relationship between what is said and what is meant and the relationship between what is said and what is known. Irony comes into play when these relationships are marked by significant discrepancies. The discrepancy between what is said and what is meant is essential for verbal irony and the discrepancy between what is said and what is known is fundamental to dramatic (or narrative) irony. If and how these two kinds of irony belong together, however, is a moot point and one of the questions to be addressed by our symposium. Thus the unequal distribution of knowledge (between characters and/or between characters and the reader) which marks narrative and dramatic irony may be related to the divergence which characterizes verbal irony. When Viola in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, disguised as a boy, says to Orsino: "I am all the daughters of my father's house," Orsino, who believes Viola to be a young man, must regard this statement as verbal irony on Viola's part. What is said ("daughters") is very different from what appears to be meant ("sons"). To us, the audience, however, this is a case of dramatic irony since we know that Viola is a woman and we observe Orsino's ignorance. What makes this case particularly intriguing is that here dramatic irony is not based on a discrepancy between what is said and what we know since Viola literally speaks the truth. The discrepancy arises between what we know and what is supposed to be spoken ironically. The example shows that asking about the relationship between verbal and dramatic/narrative irony entails numerous other questions that the Connotations symposium is going to address. In particular, we will ask about effects of irony, both with regard to characters and the audience. What is the added value of an ironic remark? What does it tell us about the speaker? In what way does an ironic utterance signal that there is a common ground between the communication partners? Are the inclusion and exclusion of others, i.e. those who get the ironical meaning and those who don't, similar to cases of discrepant awareness? How do we know that an utterance is meant ironically and how are we to deal with ambiguity in this respect? Can non-verbal irony markers be encoded in literary texts? Are theories of verbal irony based on notions of echo and pretence relatable to drama and fiction? We invite papers focussing on these and related questions, based on literature in English from the Middle Ages to the present. Please send an abstract (300 words max.) to the editors of Connotations at symposium2027@connotations.de by 31 October 2026

items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). Table of Contents Section 1: Hip-Hop: A Cultural Politic Chapter 1: The Context of Hip-Hop's Roots and Routes in the Early 1970s Chapter 2: Political Movements that Impacted Hip-Hop's Foundation Chapter 3: Hip-Hop's Formal Political Movements like "Rock the Vote" Chapter 4: Hip-Hop and Moral Panic Section 2: Hip-Hop Generating Identity Chapter 5: Hip-Hop and Generational Identity in the "Post-Racial" Era Chapter 6: Obama, Neoliberalism, and Hip-Hop Mainstream Partisan Politics Chapter 7: From "FDT" to Kodak Black: Hip-Hop's Complicated Relationship with Trump Chapter 8: Hip-Hop and the Black Lives Matter Movement Chapter 9: "Alright" and Social Protests Against Police Brutality Section 3: Hip-Hop and the Sports-Industrial Complex Chapter 10: A History of the Relationship Between Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 11: Subculture to Spectacle: The Evolution of Breaking and Olympic Institutionalization Chapter 12: Ice Cube, The Big Three, and Mogul "Activism" Chapter 13: Jay-Z and the Problematics of the Roc Nation-NFL Partnership Section 4: Representing: Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 14: The Politics of Aesthetics: Street Fashion, the Tunnel Walk, and Racialized Pleasure Chapter 15: Generational Agency: From Michael Jordan's Brand to LeBron's "Representation Activism" Chapter 16: The WNBA and Queering Hip-Hop Aesthetics Chapter 17: Hip-Hop Dance as Art and Sport

items.fullDescription: Mythology in Contemporary Culture at the Annual Conference of the Popular Culture Association Boston Marriott Copley Place March 24-27, 2027 The Mythology in Contemporary Culture area is dedicated to exploring mythological stories, figures and themes from all cultures and historical periods in all areas of popular culture. The frequent appearance of mythological motifs in popular culture speaks to the notion that mythologies, far from being relics of the past, continue to have significance. Contemporary revisionings and reinterpretations of mythological elements reflect the attitudes of current culture. Movies, television, gaming, comics, graphic novels, traditional literature, visual arts, performing arts, politics, blogs-the list goes on--hold both explicit and implicit renderings of archetypes such as Athena, Thor, Kali, and Maui, and of mythological narratives such as those found in bodies of sacred literature, classical Greek tragedies, medieval Grail legends, and culture hero narratives to name only a few examples. Proposals that pertain to the general theme of Mythology in Contemporary Culture are welcome. Potential presenters seeking inspiration for a paper topic might reflect on mythological aspects trending in media and entertainment, political currents around the world, the many "-isms" that underlie discrimination of all kinds, or the mythological aspects of a specific place (such as Boston). We will consider proposals for individual papers and/or panels organized around a theme. Sessions are 90 minutes, typically with four presenters per session. Presentations should not exceed 15 minutes. All submissions must be made through the conference submission site https://pcaaca.org/page/submissionguidelines Potential presenters must be current, paid, members of the PCA to submit proposals for the conference.For individual papers, please submit a title and 100-250 word abstract. items.fullDescription: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. In this way, the theory provides the “genus” of which a given film will be a mere “species”. The application of psychoanalytic ideas or Marxist concepts to film would therefore run the risk of depriving the specificity and singularity of the object in favour of the hegemony of the theory. Here, theory would truly live up to its theological vocation (the “theo” in theory refers to God) standing transcendentally above its “object” upon which it would cast its daunting shadow.

items.title: Travelling Cultural Heritage. Circulation and Digital Afterlives
items.location: Sibiu, Romania · Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu
items.excerpt: Travelling Cultural Heritage Circulation and Digital Afterlives Call for Papers Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference 4th edition Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Romania December 10-11, 2026 Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, as part of the FORTHEM Alliance, invites scholars, researchers, and practitioners to submit proposals for the 4th edition...
items.fullDescription: Travelling Cultural Heritage Circulation and Digital Afterlives Call for Papers Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference 4th edition Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Romania December 10-11, 2026 Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, as part of the FORTHEM Alliance, invites scholars, researchers, and practitioners to submit proposals for the 4th edition of the Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference, dedicated to exploring cultural heritage as a dynamic process of circulation across cultural, geographical, institutional, and historical boundaries. The 2026 edition focuses on Travelling Cultural Heritage (TCH): an approach that understands heritage not as a fixed repository, but as a process through which cultural forms, practices, ideas, and meanings move, encounter different contexts, and are transformed along the way. Drawing on Edward Said's concept of "travelling theory", Mieke Bal's "travelling concepts", and scholarship on cultural circulation, TCH shifts attention from mobile objects to the processes through which heritage is transmitted, adapted, appropriated, reinterpreted, and re-signified. Heritage travels through migration, exchange, conquest, education, trade, tourism, collecting, translation, transmedial transfer, and institutional networks. Migrants adapt cultural practices acquired abroad to their home contexts; travelling elites import fashions, recipes, and other cultural products; artistic styles acquire regional forms as they circulate; and networks of institutions, scholars, dealers, and historical circumstances determine how artefacts enter major collections. Such movements involve adaptation and transformation, but also appropriation, exclusion, and unequal centre-periphery relations. Circulation may allow heritage to acquire new meanings, but it may also entail loss. The large-scale purchase, digitisation, and destruction of books for AI training suggests a future in which physical heritage disappears while its digital avatars survive-an extreme form of travel across media and material states, combining virtual preservation with material destruction. More optimistically, AI, data science, interoperable infrastructures, and spatial visualisation can trace cultural circulation, compare contexts, and recover seemingly lost artefacts, including previously unreadable ancient manuscripts. We welcome contributions that engage with Travelling Cultural Heritage from disciplinary and interdisciplinary perspectives, including cultural and heritage studies, anthropology, archaeology, sociology, history, linguistics and literary studies, political science, art history, architecture, digital humanities, economics, media studies, religious studies, drama, film, the performing arts, museum studies, memory studies, and food studies . Contributors are invited to submit abstracts on, but not limited to, the following themes: Travelling Cultural Heritage: theories, concepts, and methodologies; Cultural circulation, transmission, adaptation, and re-signification; Heritage: migration, displacement, and diaspora; Museums, collections, objects, routes, networks, intermediaries, and infrastructures of cultural circulation; The movement of architectural forms, artistic practices, rituals, and cultural traditions; Colonial, postcolonial, and decolonial circulations of cultural heritage; Digital heritage, digital infrastructures, AI, platforms and computational approaches to cultural circulation; Heritage in translation: what changes when cultural forms travel between languages and the production of new heritage meanings Local content, foreign forms: adaptation and naturalisation across literatures; World Cultural Heritage: comparative approaches to heritage beyond national frameworks; Archaeological evidence for mobility, exchange, and cultural contacts; Memory and heritage: overlappings and differences; Case studies of cultural forms, practices, objects, ideas, or meanings that have travelled across contexts. Submission Guidelines Please submit an abstract of 250-300 words , along with a short biographical note ( max. 100 words ), to Ovio Olaru ( ovio.olaru@ulbsibiu.ro ) and Daniela Stanciu-P?sc?ri?a ( daniela.stanciu@ulbsibiu.ro ) by November 1, 2026. The organisers' decision regarding submissions will be communicated by November 15. For effectiveness, please include " Cultural Heritage Lab conference submission " in the subject line of your email. The conference will be held in English, German, and French, and will take place exclusively on-site. We look forward to your contributions! Kind regards, The organisers

items.title: International Symposium: The Embodiment of Trauma in Artistic Practices
items.excerpt: Call for contributions: International Symposium organized by Nordic Summer University February 24-26, 2027 - Vilnius, Lithuania in collaboration with the Center for Psychotraumatology at Vilnius University,Performative Design Association, Luna16 Community Resource Center & Feminist Art Space ASABA The winter symposium of our NSU study circle is centered o...
items.fullDescription: Call for contributions: International Symposium organized by Nordic Summer University February 24-26, 2027 - Vilnius, Lithuania in collaboration with the Center for Psychotraumatology at Vilnius University,Performative Design Association, Luna16 Community Resource Center & Feminist Art Space ASABA The winter symposium of our NSU study circle is centered on trauma as an embodied and contested concept, and artistic practices as forms of knowledge production. We are particularly interested in how art engages with experiences of trauma beyond representation, and how bodies carry, transmit, remember, resist, and transform individual and collective histories. Theme: The Embodiment of Trauma in Artistic Practices Contemporary art has become an important site for exploring the embodiment of memory, violence, displacement, ecological loss, and collective histories. Across practices, artists increasingly investigate experiences that exceed language and resist fixed interpretation. Rather than merely representing trauma, these practices generate new ways of sensing, remembering, witnessing, resisting, and imagining together. The symposium approaches trauma as a contested concept. While informed by contemporary research in psychology, and neuroscience, it recognizes that no single discipline can fully account for how trauma is lived, embodied, remembered, or transmitted. Clinical and diagnostic frameworks have significantly contributed to understanding traumatic experiences, yet they also exist within broader institutional, political, and economic systems that shape whose suffering becomes visible, whose experiences are legitimized, and which forms of care are recognized. At a moment when concepts such as healing, resilience, and post-traumatic growth are increasingly mobilized within cultures of productivity, self-optimization, and return to normative functioning, the symposium asks what artistic practice can offer beyond narratives of repair. Questions that explore this inquiry include: ? How does trauma become embodied, and what can artistic practices reveal about this relationship? ? How are trauma, memory, and embodiment shaped by colonization, occupation, war, displacement, ecological crisis, extraction, systemic oppression, interpersonal violence, and intergenerational histories? ? How can artistic practices create spaces for mourning, care, resistance, coexistence, and collective imagination beyond dominant narratives of healing and self-optimization? ? What forms of knowledge emerge through movement, performance, ritual, material practices, sound, image, and other embodied forms? ? How can art challenge dominant narratives of pathology and create alternative ways of living with difficult histories? - Call for contributions We invite artists, researchers, filmmakers, performers, scholars, activists, body practitioners, communities of care, psychologists, and people with lived experience to enrich our dialogue. A diversity of formats is welcome and we highly encourage practice-based forms to present and share research. These include: community-based workshops, body movement practices, moving image, sound, socially engaged practices, walks, and experimental or hybrid formats. We particularly welcome perspectives emerging from marginalized, feminist, queer, diasporic, disabled, and community-based practices. Submit to: decolonialstudycircle@gmail.com Title; Format description; Abstract (max. 250 words); Bionote (max. 100 words). Participation & Registration Participation is only in person for participants residing in Europe. Participants outside Europe may present online with a reduced €50 NSU membership fee. ? €60 - Reduced-rate fee (50 euros membership towards NSU, 10 euros towards our study circle)* ? €150 - Standard fee (100 euros membership towards NSU, 50 euros towards our study circle)** ? €250 - Supporting membership (150 euros membership towards NSU, 100 euros towards our study circle)*** *The reduced-rate fee is for individuals with an annual income below €25,000, as well as students, early-career researchers, retired, unemployed, working in precarious or low- income circumstances. **The standard fee is for individuals with an annual income between €25,000 and €50,000. ***The supporting membership fee is for individuals with an annual income above €50,000, as well as institutions or individuals whose membership is funded by their institution, employer, or research grant. Part of the funds from our study circle will go towards printing a participatory glossary on trauma. Key dates Submission deadline: November 1, 2026, 23:59 AoE (Anywhere on Earth). Notification of acceptance: November 15, 2026. Symposium dates: 24-26 February, 2027. Read the full call here: https://www.nsuweb.org/circle-3-re-configuring-colonialities-reforging-knowledges-healing-trauma-and-re-imagining-digital-futures/ Can't join us in person? Contribute a question. If the theme resonates with you but you're unable to attend, we invite you to submit a question for the roundtable discussion. The roundtable will bring together psychologists, researchers, artists, and community-based practitioners, and is open to a range of topics. The roundtable will be broadcasted and recorded. items.excerpt: Consuming US Popular Culture: Media Aesthetics, Ethics and Literacy Virtual Conference | 27-28 November 2026 The consumption of popular culture and media, particularly through platforms and social networks, has become one of the most common leisure time activities worldwide, and US productions are one of the most circulated. items.fullDescription: Consuming US Popular Culture: Media Aesthetics, Ethics and Literacy Virtual Conference | 27-28 November 2026 The consumption of popular culture and media, particularly through platforms and social networks, has become one of the most common leisure time activities worldwide, and US productions are one of the most circulated. Television series, films, videogames, TikTokers, podcasters, memes and other forms of digital culture reach global audiences and shape political identities and cultural imaginaries. Far from being mere entertainment, these texts have consequently become intertwined and virtually inseparable from the daily practices through which individuals get their news input and even their education. The purpose of this year's virtual conference is to open a space for the analysis of the ethical principles (or lack thereof) that seem to guide the construction, circulation and reception of public discourses within the popular culture ecosystem, including both more traditional mediums such as television and comics, but also the products that emerge from generative AI. Popular media content exists as a key source of information in public discourse and influences how we interpret contemporary political issues, how we teach and learn, and even how we exist and behave in society. Although media effects have long been proven to be negotiated rather than direct, the understanding of desirable aesthetics, mindless entertainment and the rhetoric used in political discussions have been hugely impacted by AI generated content. With this cultural media environment in mind, this virtual conference invites explorations of US popular culture through the perspective of media ethics, media literacy and aesthetics. We aim at establishing a space of discussion on the political, educational, ethical and social implications of contemporary media consumption through the analysis of US popular culture. The conference welcomes contributions that tackle the ethical dimensions and societal impact of US popular culture across a wide range of media forms and how they operate within the fragmented and algorithmically curated media ecosystem that we inhabit. We welcome analysis of both mainstream and independent productions, historical and contemporary texts, as well as emerging digital practices. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: × Media ethics and the social responsibilities of producers, platforms and audiences × Media literacy as a framework for analyzing contemporary popular culture × Popular culture as a case study for developing media literacy, ethical reasoning and critical thinking in education × The teaching potential behind popular media texts × Media effects and audience reception of US popular culture × Social media trends, influencers and memes × AI aesthetics in popular media × Polarization, misinformation, conspiracy narratives, and the circulation of disinformation through popular media × (Un)ethical representation of minorities × Political communication, civic engagement, and democratic participation through entertainment media × Representation of political and social problems in US popular culture Deadline for proposals: 1 November 2026 We accept abstract proposals for individual presentations (≈ 250 words), as well as full panels (3 presenters, ≈ 250-word description of the panel plus brief abstracts of all papers). Please, submit your abstract proposal via email at popmec.media@gmail.com as a single attachment (.doc, .docx, .odt) including name, affiliation (if any), and contact email.
