items.fullDescription: Arconexiones. Graduate conference of the Spanish Master's students of the Department of Anthropology and Languages at ISU Cartographies, Spaces and Borders: Exploring Limits and Possibilities "Borders are set up to define the places that are safe and unsafe, to distinguish us from them. A border is a dividing line, a narrow strip along a steep edge. A borderland is a vague and undetermined place created by the emotional residue of an unnatural boundary. It is a constant state of transition. The prohibited and forbidden are its inhabitants." -Gloria Anzaldúa "Nothing suggests the feeling of boundless spaces quite like silence" -Gastón Bachelard Virtual Idaho State University Saturday, February 20, 2027 9am-4pm Mountain Time (GMT-7) Keynotes: Dr. Abel Arango Skidmore College Luis Benavides Idaho State University In considering this year's theme, the conference organizers propose an exploration of spaces and borders-both in their physical and conceptual dimensions. Maps, as a starting point, offer us not only a visual version of the world we inhabit but also reflect our perspectives, what we value, and how humans seek to control, separate, and name these spaces. They contain clues regarding political and military history, conflicts, and abuses of power. To take possession of these territories, the Europeans who arrived in the Americas often described these lands in great detail-creating, in effect, maps made of words. For their part, the Indigenous peoples of these lands possess their own ways of understanding their spaces, which are deeply rooted in their cultural values. We see spaces under control, spaces that bear different names depending on the culture or language, spaces that are private, public, or shared-and an endless variety of ways to conceive of them. The work "América Invertida" ("Inverted America")-an ink drawing by the Uruguayan artist Joaquín Torres García-offers an inspiring perspective, presenting the South American continent as viewed from the south. Another significant contemporary map is the "Equal Earth" projection, adopted by the United Nations in September 2026, which provides a more accurate representation of the actual size of the continents. Maps have long been a fixture on the walls and in the textbooks of our schools; they shape the initial concept of the nation for young citizens. We invite you to explore the idea of space in all its forms - beyond both the geographical and the physical - and to enter into the realm of liminality, the transitional states between two places, the boundaries between disciplines or genres, and the marginality of certain groups or individuals. Can one feel, through cultural productions, a sense of belonging - or not belonging - to certain spaces? Do these cultural productions create new spaces for their readers, even though those spaces are fictional? Literary spaces are often reflections of our desires or fears, or our imaginations grappling with oppressive reality as a form of escape. Consider the famous, and sometimes magical, settings of Hispanic literature, such as Macondo, Comala, José Martí's "Our America," Al-Ándalus, or La Mancha. They linger in the mind long after we finish reading, and we continue to explore them. In this sense, for the fourth edition of the Arconexiones conference, we invite graduate and advanced undergraduate students from ISU and other universities to present work in fields such as film, literature, cultural studies, theater, pedagogy, critical theory, social studies, visual arts, music, and performance. We seek submissions that reflect on the concepts of cartographies, spaces, and borders within the context of Peninsular, Latin American, and Latinx cultural production. The goal of this gathering is to analyze how literary narratives, artistic productions, and diverse cultural expressions contribute to the construction or destruction of new borders. Suggested thematic areas include, but are not limited to: Critical cartographies and counter-cartographies: History of cartography; colonial and post-colonial maps; participatory mapping; community and Indigenous mapping; social, queer, and feminist cartographies. Social production of space: Territories, places, and landscapes; contested territories; urban and rural spaces; geographies of memory and extractivism. Borders, boundaries, and contact zones: National, internal, and symbolic borders; border regions; migration, displacement, and mobility; walls, checkpoints, and crossings; hybrid and liminal spaces (e.g. Nepantla). Cultural representations of space: Literature, film, art, and photography; imaginary maps and narratives of territory (e.g., Macondo, Comala, or La Mancha); ekphrastic descriptions of maps in literature; toponymy and soundscapes. Spatial technologies and digital humanities: Geographic Information Systems (GIS); remote sensing; digital cartography; open data; artificial intelligence and surveillance; ethics of geographic data. Construction of national identities and nations: such as Benedict Anderson's concept of "Imagined Communities," nation-building following independence, and also in Doris Sommer's "Foundational Fictions." Spaces, environment, and futures: the climate crisis; watersheds; oceans, and amphibious territories; transboundary spaces and governance; cartographies of the Anthropocene. Innovations in pedagogy and linguistics: Spanglish as a tool for identity; borders and contact zones between languages ??(code-switching, translanguaging); barriers to acquisition and/or learning; new linguistic spaces created on social media and the Internet that challenge geographic boundaries; taking language learning beyond the classroom walls (experiential learning or virtual learning). Interested applicants can submit a 200-250 word abstract of their original research work (or proposal) and with a title. Presentations will be accepted in English or Spanish, lasting 15 minutes (approximately 8 pages double-spaced), with additional time for questions and comments. The deadline for submissions is Monday, December 7th, 2026. For more information, contact us at marinlaufenberg@isu.edu or visit the conference website: https://www.isu.edu/anthropology/student-experience/arconexiones-conferenceconferencia/ Send your proposals using this link before Monday, December 7th, 2026-- https://forms.gle/Jy4SPKbsjDwBQYWc7

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters: One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft For thousands of years, embroidery and embroidered work have been used as a mode of visual storytelling and of documenting national or cultural histories. From the 12000 years-old fiberwork found in the Guitarrero Cave, to twine textile artwork of the Peruvian Norte Chico civilization of 2500 BCE, the thousands of years old Chinese silk thread embroidery, the decorative thread arts of the Indus Valley Civilization of 3000 BCE, the ancient Egyptian needlework of 1300 BCE, the Bayeux Tapestry of Norman conquest, and the thousands of years old embroidery and quilt work of the indigenous communities across the North and South Americas, human civilizations have woven and embroidered their histories and cultures and have archived everything for future generations. Embroidery has also functioned as a powerful trope of resistance narrative and rebellious vision. Marjorie Agosín's iconic book, Tapestries of Hope recounts how Chilean women used embroidery and textile art as tools of resistance and rebellion during Pinochet's dictatorship. More recently, Kirstie McLeod's collaborative project "The Red Dress" brings together the needlework, voices, and stories of 380 individuals from 51 countries. Collectively, their embroidered experiences on a single red dress, across a range of expertise, positions, and languages, testify to human rights concerns around the world. In the context of underprivileged women from the global South, embroidery and needlework have been a source of financial freedom and a platform for women's social bonding and personal expressions. For example, cottage industries in Bangladesh, India, and many other South and East Asian countries have mobilized economically impoverished women into an active workforce and have turned embroidery and needlework into a booming business. In literature and media, embroidered works also provide intense narrative power. Adrienne Rich's "Aunt Jennifer's Tigers" and Rosa del Valle's tablecloth in Isabel Allende's The House of the Spirits, are two such examples. Embroidery has provided a pertinent motif for re-presenting folklore, myth, and collective memory in many countries, such as Bangladesh and India, where women's acts of illustrating folklores, personal loss and pain in quilts or narrating the mythical stories of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata through needlework are an essential part of their national and cultural history. Textile arts, embroidery and needlework function as narrative technologies that initiate individual, social, and political involvement. It invokes memory and provokes individuals to make or break myths regarding nation, narration, gender, identity, and/or human existence in the age of artificial intelligence. Against this extensive backdrop of embroidery as a narrative technology, we invite abstracts for a collection tentatively titled One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft. Tentative topic list for the paper (but is not limited to): Archiving history through embroidery Embroidery as narrative technology Embroidery as a trope of Agency and/or Identity Embroidery as a narrative of political resistance Embroidery as Storytelling Embroidery and human rights or social justice Embroidery and activism Embroidery and/in literature Embroidery and/as cultural identity Embroidery and/as visual narrative Embroidery and ecocriticism Myth, memory, and embroidery Retelling myth and re-presenting identity Women and embroidery Please send us your 150 words abstract with 3 key words and a 50-word bio by December 10, 2026. If accepted, we will request for the completed essay (minimum of 7000 words) by June 30, 2027. The anthology is expected to be published by a university press in the US. Looking forward to receiving your abstract at fayeza.hasanat@ucf.edu , cc farrah.cato@ucf.edu Sincerely, Dr. Fayeza Hasanat and Dr. Farrah Cato English Department University of Central Florida

items.fullDescription: "Creativity, Resistance and Social Change" International Conference 27-28 February 2027 St Anne's College, University of Oxford & Online organised by London Centre for Interdisciplinary Research Across history and cultures, creativity has played a central role in resisting injustice, challenging dominant narratives and imagining alternative social futures. From storytelling, music and visual art to literature, performance, digital media and everyday creative practices, acts of creation often emerge in response to exclusion, oppression or crisis. Creativity can unite communities, give voice to marginalised experiences and sustain collective struggles for dignity, justice and transformation. This conference invites interdisciplinary reflections on how creative practices function as forms of resistance and catalysts for social change. We welcome contributions that explore creativity both as an expressive response to power and as an active force shaping social, political and cultural transformations. Possible themes Include (but are not limited to): Creativity as resistance and dissent Storytelling, memory and counter-narratives Oral traditions, folklore and cultural transmission Literature, poetry and narrative activism Music, performance and protest cultures Visual arts, street art and public space Digital creativity, social media and online resistance Youth cultures, creativity and social movements Gender, sexuality and creative resistance Indigenous, postcolonial and decolonial creative practices Creativity, migration, displacement and belonging Art, trauma, healing and social repair Creative economies, labour and social justice Education, pedagogy and creativity for social change We welcome submissions from across the humanities and social sciences, including but not limited to literature, anthropology, sociology, history, cultural studies, media and communication, psychology, education, political science and the arts. Proposals may take the form of: Individual papers Panel or roundtable proposals Practice-based or creative presentations Community-engaged or participatory research Paper proposals up to 250 words and a brief biographical note should be sent by 15 December 2026 to: creative-voices@lcir.co.uk.

items.fullDescription: In her book Bodyminds Reimagined , Sami Schalk asks us “What might it mean to imagine disability differently?” (2) Her work, situated in the exploration of black speculative fiction, engages with (dis)ability studies and black feminism to gesture toward a reimagining of what Margaret Price termed the ‘bodymind’, a concept predicated on “the enmeshment of the mind and body.” (5) How might this enmeshment be understood in the context of chronic conditions, themselves experienced as a direct result of climate change and biomedical violence? Is the planet - made sick by extractive capitalism and anthropogenic action as Shukla, Settee, Lincoln and others claim - now existing in a state of (dis)ability?

items.fullDescription: DH 2.0: Transdisciplinary Conversations on Digital Humanities A Hybrid International Conference organized by AIESR, Amity University, Noida Pre-Conference Workshops on 02 March 2027 Conference on 03-05 March 2027 (Online and In-Person) Digital Humanities Quarterly, in the early 2000s, described Digital Humanities as an emerging field practising humanities research in and through information technology, exploring how the humanities "may evolve through their engagement with technology, media, and computational methods". More recently JHU Arts and Science Magazine and University College Cork has developed a broader definitional field for Digital Humanities, alluding to the generic use of "digital or computer-based technology to expand knowledge" across Humanities disciplines. Following these articulations, past DH projects have ranged from the curation of digital archives and literary editions, computational linguistics or literary studies, text mining, mapping and spatial humanities, to museum preservation, Network Analysis, and Educational AI use. Presently, Digital Humanities remains indicative of a transdisciplinary field that includes the use of practices such as digital data archiving, text mining, corpus linguistics, GIS mapping, data visualisation, cultural informatics, machine learning, digital editing, and artificial intelligence to study and analyse history, literature, philosophy, art history, archaeology, cognitive science, and cultural and heritage studies. This DH 2.0 International Conference entitled "Transdisciplinary Conversations on Digital Humanities" - the second instalment of the AIESR DH initiative - does not simply invite students, scholars, educators, and industry specialists to draw on such an existing corpus of projects, edited volumes, monographs, and digital archives but insists that they submit inspiring and innovative work that challenges the limits of the field. On this basis, DH 2.0, a hybrid conference organized by AIESR and scheduled on 02-05 March 2027, are seeking abstracts from undergraduates, postgraduates, research scholars, faculty members and industry experts in the following tracks. Track I: Digital Humanities, Literary Studies, Cultural Studies, and Video Game Studies Track II: Digital Humanities and Theoretical, Applied, and Computational Linguistics Track III: Digital Humanities, Translation Studies, and Comparative Literature Track IV: Digital Humanities, AI and Philosophy of Ethics Track V: Digital Humanities and Cognitive Science Track VI: Digital Humanities, Pedagogy, and Education Policy These tracks only remain suggestive of the kind of scholarship we are soliciting, and do not exhaust the possible topics we are prepared to entertain. Moreover, shortlisted presenters will be later asked to submit full-length manuscripts of their work, which will be compiled in an edited volume and published by an academic publisher of international repute. Please submit your abstracts (of up to 350 words) by accessing the google form here: https://forms.gle/Kndg68GeJHLypGGi8 Important Dates Start of Abstract Submission 30 October 2026 Abstract Submission Deadline 20 December 2026 Intimation of Abstract Acceptance 05 January 2027 Registration Deadline for DH 2.0 15 February 2027 DH 2.0 Conference 02-05 March 2027 Shortlist for Full Manuscript. 18 April 2027

items.title: Hydrotemporalities: Situating the spatial and temporal presence of water in historical, contemporary, and future perspectives
items.excerpt: Hydrotemporalities: Situating the spatial and temporal presence of water in historical, contemporary, and future perspectives: Student Conference, Early Career Researchers Opportunity The 'Hydro' in Hydrotemporalities draws from the Blue Humanities, a term coined by Steve Mentz in 2024, and more specifically from Astrida Neimanis' notion of Hydrofeminism...
items.fullDescription: Hydrotemporalities: Situating the spatial and temporal presence of water in historical, contemporary, and future perspectives: Student Conference, Early Career Researchers Opportunity The 'Hydro' in Hydrotemporalities draws from the Blue Humanities, a term coined by Steve Mentz in 2024, and more specifically from Astrida Neimanis' notion of Hydrofeminism and the collection Thinking with Water (eds. Astrida Neimanis, Cecilia Chen, and Janine MacLeod). As such, the 'Hydro' means to evoke and underline the ever growing importance of watery topics and posthumanism in the academic discourse, and is specifically indicative of the intersectional approach of the conference: As Mentz and Neimanis remind us, water is what connects all the world, water facilitates movement, growth, thinking, and loving, and water acts as a planetary archive. Further, we use 'Hydro' to mean water-based fluids of all kinds, in all its states, because we are interested in the different forms and meanings that it can take. It encompasses all bodies of water both artificial and natural, the polar caps, fog, rain, and even sewage. Temporalities refer to chronology; future, past, history, speculative time, and more. It can come to mean the temporal levels of a narrative, the way the past informs the present, the speculative presence of the future, scientific advancements and historical processes. Further, temporality necessitates a negotiation of place and space, seeing as the temporal must be situated within the spatial, in the tradition of Bakhtin's chronotopos. The spatial is not limited to physical places, but includes fictional/unreal and social/cultural spaces. In combining these two, we wish to uncover the role water and fluids play in the literary, historical, futuristic, scientific, and artistic chronologies and spaces of humanity, especially in regards to our current era of the Anthropocene and the changing climate. 'Hydro' situates itself in every aspect of the world. Our aim is to facilitate a productive exchange between different disciplines and give early career researchers the opportunity to build a supportive network. Disciplines and Topics can include but are not limited to: cultural and literary studies linguistics historical and archaeological perspectives art and art history natural sciences, such as biology, geology, ecology, and more philosophy, sociology, and political science geography narrative structures/cyclical narratives materiality and representation of water reconsidering the legacy of slavery/discussions of the middle passage water in all its states (steam/ice/fluid) ecocritical readings the polar caps/arctic imaginaries climate change/climate fiction the Anthropocene/posthumanism We welcome submissions from all kinds of early career researchers at BA, MA, and early PhD level. All disciplines are encouraged, as long as your idea fits the topic. The conference will be held in English. You may submit abstracts to present a paper you've already written or a paper in progress, but you can also send in concepts of a workshop, or any kind of creative presentation, such as fiction, art, movies, or music. If you're unsure about your idea or have any questions, don't hesitate to contact Helena Kreuzmann at kreuzmann@anglistik.uni-kiel.de. We will do our best to support you. The abstract should be between 250 and 400 words long. Please include a bio-note of around 100 to 150 words. The presentations will be 20 minutes long. The deadline for submitting your abstracts is 20.12.2026 . Please send your abstracts to Mina Hesse at hesse@anglistik.uni-kiel.de . We will contact you by early February to let you know whether you have been accepted. The conference will take place 02. - 03.04.2027 in Kiel. If you are not able to make the trip, participation over Zoom is possible. Selected Bibliography: Bakhtin, Mikhail (1981). The Dialogic Imagination, transl. Michael Holquist. Austin/London: University of Texas Press. Braidotti, R. , Jones, E. , & Klumbyt?, G. (Ed.). (2022). More Posthuman Glossary. London: Bloomsbury [http://dx.doi.org/10.5040/9781350231467]. Foucault, Michel (1984). Of Other Spaces: Utopias and Heterotopias. Massachusetts Institute of Technology [https://web.mit.edu/allanmc/www/foucault1.pdf]. Haraway, Donna (2016). Staying with the Trouble: Making Kin in the Chthulucene. Durham/London: Duke University Press. Lefebvre, Henri (1991) The Production of Space, transl. Donald Nicholson-Smith. Oxford/Cambridge:Blackwell.[https://iberian-connections.yale.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/4/The-production-of-space-by-Henri-Lefebvre-translated-by-Donald-Nicholson-Smith.pdf] Mentz, Steve (2024). An Introduction to Blue Humanities. New York/London: Routledge. Neimanis, Astrida, Chen, Cecilia, MacLeod, Janine (2013). Thinking with Water. London/Ithaca: McGill-Queen's University Press. Neimanis, Astrida (2017). Bodies of Water: Posthuman Feminist Phenomenology. London: Bloomsbury Academic. [http://dx.doi.org/10.5040/9781474275415]. Ricoeur, Paul (1980). Narrative Time. Critical Inquiry, 7(1), 169-190. [http://www.jstor.org/stable/1343181].

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers Yearbook KRIEG UND LITERATUR/WAR AND LITERATURE VOL. 32 (2027) (Göttingen: V&R unipress/Universitätsverlag Osnabrückpublished since 1989 and as a yearbook since 2000; distributed to subscribers worldwide) Invisible Fronts - Representations of War between AI, Disinformation, and Hybrid Warfare Wars have never been fought solely on military battlefields. Cyber operations, social media, automated weapons systems, algorithmic decision-making processes, and generative artificial intelligence have transformed warfare in recent decades-as well as its media representation and public perception. Disinformation, surveillance, and the deliberate manipulation of public perception are increasingly blurring the lines between war and peace, reality and simulation, and documentation and staging. The 2027 issue of KRIEG UND LITERATUR/WAR AND LITERATURE explores cultural representations of these developments. The focus is on how 20th- and 21st-century media depict, reflect on, critique, or anticipate technological and hybrid forms of warfare, and how new technologies are changing the conditions under which wars are narrated, documented, remembered, and perceived as real. Possible topics include: • AI, autonomous weapons systems, drones, and algorithmic targeting; • cyberwarfare, hybrid warfare, and digital infrastructures; • propaganda, disinformation, and deepfakes; • generative AI and synthetic images of war; • manipulation of perception, memory, and enemy stereotypes; • responsibility and agency in the relationship between humans and machines; • historical imaginaries of automated and hybrid warfare. Across all genres and formats, contributions may examine works and materials from literature, film and television, comics and graphic novels, visual and digital art, photography, social media, and video games. Interdisciplinary, comparative, and transnational approaches are also welcome. Contributions may be submitted in German or English . The following general formatting guidelines should be observed: • Submit as a WORD or RTF document; language: German or English; a maximum of 25 A4 pages (excluding illustrations); Footnotes rather than endnotes); • Figures (printed in black and white) must be submitted separately as offset film, a reproducible original, or in digital format (*.tif, *.jpg with at least 300 dpi in CMYK mode). Please mark the location in the text where each figure is to appear. Do not embed the figures in the document; • Include correct and complete figure captions in the text or in a separate file; • Authors are responsible for obtaining all necessary reproduction permissions. Detailed "Guidelines for Authors" will be sent separately. Abstracts : 1,500-2,000 characters (including spaces) Deadline for abstract submissions : December 31, 2026 Notification of acceptance : January 31, 2027 Deadline for full paper submission : June 30, 2027 Paper length : 15-25 pages Contact and Submission : Claudia Junk, M.A. and Alice Cadeddu, M.A. (Editors) Email: junk@osnabrueck.de; cadeddu@osnabrueck.de Erich Maria Remarque Peace Center; www.remarque.de

items.title: [Edited book] Handbook of National Revolutions. National Revolutions in the World: Theories, Practices, International Relations
items.excerpt: Beginning in the nineteenth century, the world witnessed the emergence of national movements that advocated the construction of states founded upon the historical and cultural identity of peoples, as well as upon their independence and strategic autonomy. This wave, which manifested itself most prominently in the European revolutions of 1848, the so-calle...
items.fullDescription: Beginning in the nineteenth century, the world witnessed the emergence of national movements that advocated the construction of states founded upon the historical and cultural identity of peoples, as well as upon their independence and strategic autonomy. This wave, which manifested itself most prominently in the European revolutions of 1848, the so-called "Springtime of the Peoples," produced a long-term historical impact - according to the principle of the longue durée - that influenced world political history in the decades that followed. This phenomenon was of enormous importance in the Western political sphere, having its precursors in the American Revolution and in the political epic of South American Bolivarianism, and gaining momentum from 1848 onward with the emergence of a whole series of European national movements. With the First World War, and with the promotion by Woodrow Wilson and the United States of the principle of "self-determination of peoples," the same idea experienced a revival which, through Turkish Kemalism and the formation of the Chinese nationalist movement, extended into the non-Western world. Non-Western forms of this type of movement, in turn, had important precursors in anti-colonial movements, which, like European national movements, sought to secure independence and autonomy for broad sectors of the world subjected to foreign domination of an economic and extractive nature. During the twentieth century, the idea of national independence assumed various ideological and political forms, eventually giving rise to different theories of national autonomy and sovereignty, such as Mao Zedong's "Three Worlds Theory." At the same time, the rise of communist revolutions and of the world socialist camp revitalized this political idea, generating new formulations of theories of national revolution. With this call for papers, we intend to collect contributions on the theme of national revolutions in the West and the East, considered both from a theoretical perspective - by examining the political thought of the authors who promoted these movements, as well as the movements themselves - and from the perspective of the relations among these movements and the elaboration of a political theory of coexistence among these political projects. We also intend to focus on the theories and practices of these movements from the perspective of international relations, both by analyzing national revolutions within the international context, in diplomatic and strategic terms, and by addressing the theoretical elaboration of an international order founded upon national independence. A non-exhaustive list of topics that may be addressed includes: Jacobinism and the emergence of the idea of national revolution in Europe The American Revolution and the national-revolutionary paradigm Bolivarianism and national revolution in Spanish America 1848 and the transformation of the national idea in Europe Mazzini and the theory of nationalities The Italian Risorgimento and its relationship with the great powers Bonapartism and national revolutions Self-determination of peoples and the international order after the First World War Kemalism and the Turkish national revolutionù The Soviet Revolution and the issue of nationalities Chinese nationalism and national revolution in the thought of Sun Yat-sen Nationalism and anti-imperialism in anti-colonial liberation movements Mao Zedong and the theory of national revolution National revolution and internationalism in Marxist and communist thought National sovereignty, the balance of power, and the international order National identity and international relations theory National movements and the opposition to a bipolar and unipolar world National movements and anti-colonial struggles in Africa Arab nationalism and movements for emancipation in the Middle East Indian nationalism and the struggle for independence National and revolutionary movements in twentieth-century Latin America Nationalisms in Southeast Asia and the dissolution of the colonial empire Proposals should contain a title, a brief summary or abstract of between 300 and 400 words, the author's email address, and a brief five-line CV. Proposals must be sent to the email address nationalrevolutionsintheworld@gmail.com The deadline for submitting proposals is December 31, 2026. Accepted proposals will be announced starting January 31, 2027, and editorial instructions for preparing the book chapter will be provided. The deadline for submitting the final version of the chapters will be a date to be determined in the first quarter of 2027. The monograph containing the selected and submitted book chapters will subsequently be published, following corrections and comments by the coordinators. The monograph is expected to be published by an international academic publishing house. Coordinators: Orazio Maria Gnerre (Institute for the History of the Italian Risorgimento) Ruikai Xue (Beijing International Studies University)

items.fullDescription: Acta Ludologica (ISSN 2585-8599, e-ISSN 2585-9218) is a double-blind peer-reviewed scientific journal published twice a year in both online and print versions. It focuses on the comprehensive discourse of games and digital games, including theoretical and empirical studies, research results, and their implementation into practice, as well as professional publication reviews and scientific reviews of digital games. Acta Ludologica is inviting manuscripts for Vol. 10, No. 1 , scheduled to be published in June 2027. The deadline for submissions is December 31, 2026 . Journal issues include scientific reflections on digital and non-digital games, and related media and digital competencies, their creation, design, development, research, history, sociology, psychology, marketing, and the future associated with phenomena of the digital-gaming sector. The journal' regular issues are not thematically oriented, so this CFP is general for manuscripts on any topics related to games and digital games. Acta Ludologica's sections: game studies, reviews, add-ons More information about the individual journal sections, instructions for authors, as well as templates are available in the journal's Guidelines (https://actaludologica.com/guidelines/). Submitted manuscripts should strictly follow the outlined format as well as the journal's Citation Rules. Submissions are accepted only in English, with no publication fees, article-processing charges (APCs), or article submission charges. Contact and manuscript submissions: actaludologica@fmk.sk Journal's web and open access archive: www.actaludologica.com Acta Ludologica is indexed in ERIH Plus, ICI Journals Master List, Ulrich's Periodical Directory, CEEOL, and CEJSH. In addition, the journal is under the indexing process for the Emerging Sources Citation Index (ESCI) - Web of Science Core Collection.

Over years of varying interpretations, Sauron has evolved into a fi...
items.fullDescription: The Dark Lord Sauron, the titular Lord of the Rings in Tolkien’s magnum opus, plays many roles and takes many forms throughout The Lord of the Rings, The Silmarillion, and the rest of Tolkien’s Legendarium, and even more in the various adaptations and reimaginings that have since emerged. Over years of varying interpretations, Sauron has evolved into a figure of vast significance. From his early depictions as a looming, disembodied threat to his more recent portrayals as a visually captivating "sexy" villain in contemporary pop culture, Sauron’s image has undergone a transformation, revealing much about changing attitudes toward power, corruption, and desire.

items.fullDescription: How is everyone doing? At a routine meeting of the Editorial Board of this journal in March 2026, this innocuous question erupted into disquiet, tension, unease. Speaking from vastly different parts of the world, there was an unmistakable sense of a planet slipping beyond available comprehension and unplugging us from work and life routines. As wars in the Middle East expand and fires spread from apartment blocks reduced to rubble to bombed oil refineries and shipping corridors, profound geopolitical, personal, even psychic rifts leave us grasping for the language and feel of the moment, the falling apart of things, the zeitgeist of an endangered now.

items.title: Animal Studies Across Disciplines
items.location: Arizona State University · Arizona State University
items.excerpt: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pe...
items.fullDescription: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pervasive pollution. The effects of the Anthropocene have been caused by only a small percentage of the world's population, yet those living in the Global South disproportionately suffer the consequences. The Anthropocene, then, is just as much a social problem as it is an environmental issue. Despite the centrality of animals to planetary health, however, nonhuman life often remains peripheral to discussions of climate and environmental sustainability, even as industrial agriculture drives deforestation and carbon emissions, species extinction destabilizes ecosystems, and the increasing emergence of zoonotic diseases-Covid-19 and Hantavirus among them-reveals the profound interdependence of human, animal, and environmental health. At the same time, dominant responses to environmental crises, which made possible the conditions of crisis in the first place, tend to privilege scientific discovery and technological innovation while neglecting the cultural narratives, entrenched biases, and networks of power that shape human-animal relationships.. To that end, imagining more just and hospitable futures requires new interdisciplinary approaches that recognize animals and interspecies relations as critical to collective flourishing and environmental sustainability. The Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium will bring together scholars, artists, students, animal professionals, and community members across the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences to discuss animals and multispecies futures. The symposium is designed not only as a scholarly gathering, but as the start of a long-term collaborative network capable of shaping future research, public humanities work, community partnerships, and environmental dialogue. The inaugural Spring 2027 Symposium will center on the keyword "care," inviting participants to analyze how different disciplines, professions, and communities define and mobilize care in relation to animals, multispecies justice, and environmental stewardship. In doing so, the Symposium will evaluate practices of protection and responsibility alongside the violences and inequalities that shape life across species. For example, how might a humanities scholar, veterinarian, ecologist, or activist understand and practice care differently, and what might each learn from the knowledge, methods, and questions of the others? How might regional, place-based, and communal forms of knowledge offer different ways of understanding our relationships and responsibilities to animals? How is care negotiated when the welfare of an individual animal comes into conflict with the preservation of a population, species, or ecosystem? What might care mean for animals such as insects, whose small size, vast numbers, and frequent classification as pests or disease vectors complicate familiar practices of care? How do animals care for themselves, one another, and members of other species, and what might these practices teach us about caring for each other and the more-than-human world? The Symposium invites participants to consider what becomes possible when different ways of knowing and relating to animals are brought into conversation, and how such exchanges might expand our understanding and practice of care across species. Possible topics include: Regional approaches to Animal Studies and human-animal relations (e.g. desert ecologies, southern studies, the arctic, etc.) Global and transnational approaches to Animal items.title: Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy
items.excerpt: The Journal for the New Narratives in the History of Philosophy (JNNHP) invites submissions for its special on Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy, to be published in Fall 2027. Derrick Bell, the founder of Critical Race Theory, produced one of the most innovative, insightful, and transformative ideas in the 20th century. His philosophical...
items.fullDescription: The Journal for the New Narratives in the History of Philosophy (JNNHP) invites submissions for its special on Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy, to be published in Fall 2027. Derrick Bell, the founder of Critical Race Theory, produced one of the most innovative, insightful, and transformative ideas in the 20th century. His philosophical insights continue to challenge how western liberal nations contend with questions of civil rights, human rights, immigration, policing, and education. Recent conservative attacks focused on Critical Race Theory (CRT) in the U.S, Canada, and England assert, albeit erroneously, that CRT is a Marxist and communist ideology that seeks to supplant western values and the ethos of liberal democracy. Contrary to these fallacious attacks, Bell's textbook Race, Racism, and American Law is amongst the first law textbooks to give a comprehensive view of how racism shaped the development of American law and race relations. In this regard, CRT draws heavily on a tradition of Africana philosophy from slavery through the 20th century. It challenges, not only the supposed neutrality of U.S. law, but also the universality of western political ideals, and U.S. law as egalitarian. For example, Bell engaged Frederick Douglass's critiques of natural law theorists and abolitionists who read the American Constitution as a slave document. For Douglass, the Constitution is an economic contract that robs slaves of their labour and property rights. Drawing on Douglass' critique, Bell interrogated how economic interests have structured American law as an instrument for white class interests over Black claims for justice from slavery through the 20th century. Similarly, Bell engaged W.E.B DuBois's reading of American democracy that underscored how U.S. law in the 13 colonies suppressed African revolts while upholding slavery. Such legal resistance to African acts of liberation, Dubois argued, created paradoxes for American democracy and shaped how the legal system understood the Black freedom struggle. Following Dubois' analysis, Bell explored how the law is an ineffective tool for racial remediation when it comes to addressing social injustices that confront Black life. Bell also engaged Malcolm X's critiques of the Reconstruction era civil rights and 1960 civil rights amendments as pyrrhic victories. This inspired Bell to think about how civil rights function as symbolic victories while ensuring racism is a permanent fixture of American democracy. Given Bell's extensive engagement with 18th-20th century Africana philosophy, this special seeks to consider Bell's work within Africana philosophy. As such, the special welcomes essays that focus on Bell's work as philosophical historiography and inquiry into Black life and its relation to democracy as part of the long tradition of Africana philosophy. The special seeks contributions that address the following themes: Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black history. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black legal theory. Derrick Bell and the Black Nationalist and the Black Radical Tradition. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black Education. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of contemporary society and issue of civil rights. Essays must be submitted to https://journal.lib.uoguelph.ca/index.php/nnhp/about/submissions Deadline for Essay Submission: January 7th, 2027. Papers will be considered after January 7th, 2027. The Co-lead Guest Editors for this Special are Drs. Dalitso Ruwe (Queens University), Adebayo Oluwayomi (West Chester University), Andrew Soto (Hartnell College). For questions about the Special, please contact: derrickbellspecial@gmail.com JNNHP is an open-access online journal committed to publishing papers on underrepresented figures or themes in the history of philosophy, both Western and non-Western traditions, from the ancient period to the mid-20th century. JNNHP accepts papers in English and French. Papers should be no more than 10000 words. JNNHP also seeks to highlight relevant translations, archival work or new editions of primary texts in progress. We will publish selections from such works, with critical notes and contextual introductions.

items.title: Affective Worlds: Emotions and Aesthetics in Afro-Descendant Women’s Writing International Conference
items.location: Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Brussels, Belgium) · Vrije Universiteit Brussel
items.excerpt: CALL FOR PAPERS Affective Worlds: Emotions and Aesthetics in Afro-Descendant Women's Writing International Conference 24-25 May 2027, Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Belgium) Format: in person Language: English Link to the CfP : https://clic.research.vub.be/afropemotions-international-conference The conference explores the role of affect, emotions, and aesthe...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS Affective Worlds: Emotions and Aesthetics in Afro-Descendant Women's Writing International Conference 24-25 May 2027, Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Belgium) Format: in person Language: English Link to the CfP : https://clic.research.vub.be/afropemotions-international-conference The conference explores the role of affect, emotions, and aesthetics in the rich and diverse body of work published in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries by women writers of African heritage from African, European, Caribbean, and other diasporic contexts. The event examines how affect and emotions shape both the sociopolitical dimensions of Afro-descendant women's literature and its narrative and aesthetic practices across multiple linguistic, cultural, and historical contexts and through fiction, poetry, and drama. By often exploring issues of displacement, marginalisation, systemic oppression, colonial legacies, trauma, cultural memory, and environmental change, Afro-descendant women authors present affect as a site of self-awareness, resistance, community formation, and political imagination, while articulating it through narrative form, language, imagery, and other aesthetic strategies. The conference brings together established and early-career researchers working at the intersection of different fields, including affect studies, African and African diasporic literary studies, comparative literary studies, feminist and queer studies, postcolonial and decolonial studies, trauma and cultural memory studies, and the environmental humanities. While acknowledging theoretical distinctions between affect and emotion, particularly those developed in affect theory by scholars such as Tomkins (1962) and Massumi (2002), the conference welcomes literary criticism informed by diverse affective frameworks, such as cognitive and narratological perspectives on affect (e.g. Hogan 2003, 2011), sociopolitical approaches to affect and emotions (e.g. Ahmed 2004; Berlant 2011), and affective ecocriticism (e.g. Bladow and Ladino 2018). We invite papers exploring affect and emotions in Afro-descendant women's literature written in English, French, German, Italian, or other languages. Topics may include but are not limited to: Affective relations, transnational belonging, and diasporic identities Migration, displacement, and affective literary geographies Affect and gender, race, class, and sexuality Queer affects Affect, narrative form, and aesthetics Affect, language, multilingualism, and translation Emotions, trauma, and memory Collective affect, solidarity, and community formation Eco-emotions and environmental change Emotional responses to injustice, inequality, and systemic oppression Affect, embodiment, and resistance SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Please send proposals for 20-minute papers in English to Dr. Isabella Villanova (Isabella.Villanova@vub.be) and Prof. dr. Elisabeth Bekers (Elisabeth.Bekers@vub.be). Proposals should include: an abstract (max. 250 words), with up to 5 references, preferably in Chicago style; 5 keywords; a short biographical note (max. 100 words) Deadline for Proposal Submissions: 10 January 2027 Notification of Acceptance: 10 February 2027 Selected papers may be considered for publication in a special journal issue. Keynote: Prof. dr. Caroline Kögler (Freie Universität Berlin, Germany) Special Guest: Italo-Somali writer Ubah Cristina Ali Farah

This edited volume examines some of the reasons why.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS First International Congress in Humanities - Texts, Images and Communities: "Body, Age and Gender" Org. HUM-TIC Research Group, University of Madeira, 17-18 June 2017 The way in which the body, age and gender shape human experiences is one of the most pressing challenges facing contemporary societies. Today, more than ever, there is a need to build fairer, more equitable and sustainable communities, which are in a state of continuous development and adaptation and which face limitations and obstacles. Some of these are long-standing and deeply rooted, whilst others are new and not very well known. A multidisciplinary approach to the cultural and social constructs of the body - and the multiple levels at which it functions as a generator of meaning - is therefore imperative. The proposed lines of research, both in their contemporary context and in terms of their cultural and historical foundations, fall within the core mission of the Humanities Research Group - Texts, Images and Communities (HUM-TIC). This event fosters free, informed discussion, driven by dialogue across the Humanities. This is the first International Congress organised by the HUM-TIC Research Group, Faculty of Arts and Humanities at the University of Madeira. It is an in-person event, which will take place at the Colégio dos Jesuítas, at the University of Madeira's Rectorate building in Funchal. The conference aims to explore one of HUM-TIC's main thematic areas - Body, Age and Gender - from a dialogical and transdisciplinary perspective. In this context, proposals of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, are welcome across the Humanities. These may include, among others, Art, Communication, Culture, Design, History, Linguistics, Literature, Psychology and Sociology. Discussion Topics (some suggestions): - Discourses, narratives and representations of the body, age and gender. - The body, space and territoriality: real, symbolic and imaginary places. - Rethinking the Human: AI and representations of the body, age and gender. - Aesthetics of the body, beauty and ugliness, the monstrous and the abject. - Building Self and the Other in different cultural contexts. - Stages of life: representations, experiences and intergenerational relationships. - Double standards of ageing in a consumer society. - Embodiment: inner and outer, personal and social, physical and idealised. - Body and gender: sexuality, emotions, ethics, violence. - Myths, stereotypes and imagined representations of the body, age and gender. - Ecologies of the body and environmental humanities. - Gender-based violence in the digital sphere. - The manosphere and social media impact. - Intersectionality and multiple forms of discrimination. - Gender, natural disasters and climate change. Abstract Submissions: - Submission deadline: 15th January, 2027 - Working languages: Portuguese, English, Spanish - 20-minute Paper/ Panel (up to three papers): Microsoft Forms https://forms.cloud.microsoft/pages/responsepage.aspx?id=21zvRr7bJE6SsSdesroEW_Wv92T_NzBPkLLdceU3SMlUMkRYQjNBQllBTlhIT1BCRTlMQlFLWkJUMS4u&route=shorturl - Notification of acceptance: 15th February, 2027 - Conference email: 1cong.ch2027@mail.uma.pt Registration Fees: - Registration fee: €80 - MA and PhD. student registration fee: €40 - UMa lecturers and researchers registration fee: €40 - Non-speaking participants (with certificate of attendance): €10 Registration Deadlines: - Speaking participants: 30th April, 2027 - Non-speaking participants: 18th June, 2027 Location: Colégio dos Jesuítas Reitoria da Universidade da Madeira Rua dos Ferreiros, 9000-082 Funchal Madeira, Portugal Publication: Selected papers will be published in a peer-reviewed volume. items.title: "Loving Roland Barthes: An Interdisciplinary Conference"
items.location: Mobile, Alabama · University of South Alabama
items.excerpt: Call for Papers: "Loving Roland Barthes" University of South Alabama (Mobile, AL) October 14-16, 2027 Loving [Barthes], doing so in a certain fashion against the age [. . .], can only be a responsible way of living: it inevitably leads the subject who does so and says so to posit himself in his time according to the injunctions of his desire and not accor...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: "Loving Roland Barthes" University of South Alabama (Mobile, AL) October 14-16, 2027 Loving [Barthes], doing so in a certain fashion against the age [. . .], can only be a responsible way of living: it inevitably leads the subject who does so and says so to posit himself in his time according to the injunctions of his desire and not according to those of his sociality. -Roland Barthes, "Loving Schumann" Proposals for panels and papers are invited for a conference entitled "Loving Roland Barthes: Celebrating the Fiftieth Anniversary of the Publication of A Lover's Discourse: Fragments ," to be hosted by the University of South Alabama's Department of English and held at the historic Malaga Inn in downtown Mobile, city of the oldest Mardi Gras in the U.S. As conference organizers, we envision a relatively concentrated event in which scholars working in various disciplines and artists working in various genres will present new ideas about Roland Barthes, A Lover's Discourse , and his adjacent texts. This conference celebrates a peculiar form of love: an amorousness that compels the one faithful to "the specialty of [one's] desire" ( Lover's Discourse 20) to return again and again to Fragments d'un discours amoureux . Published in 1977 and translated a year later by Richard Howard as A Lover's Discourse: Fragments , Roland Barthes's tortured love song retains a strong attachment for scholars and artists alike. We might be tempted to call those strange lovers "amateurs." For, as Barthes reminded us, the word derives from "amator: one who loves and loves again" (Roland Barthes 52). Across the last five decades, the book has inspired not only articles and artwork but also autotheory, "an emergent discourse with historical precedents" (McLaughlin et al., Autotheory and Its Others 15). Often recognizable by its copious citations, autotheoretical practice pays homage to A Lover's Discourse: Fragments as one way of loving Barthes. Yet there is no limit to the modes of loving Barthes. For some, it might be collage, an assemblage of the very fragments that Barthes favored. For others, it might be singing a song (such as Annie Lennox's "No More 'I Love You's'") or writing notations (one of Barthes's preferred activities). For still others, it might be searching for "a little corner of sloth," "twiddl[ing one's] wound," or accepting "[t]he lover's fatal identity [. . .]: I am the one who waits" (Lover's Discourse 64, 161, 40). Whatever one's manner of loving Barthes, this conference invites scholars and artists to a celebration of A Lover's Discourse: Fragments . Contributions can take the form of traditional papers as well as of visual art, short film, skits, songs, and other Barthesian types of work or play. Possible topics include but are not limited to the following: · Figures and images in A Lover's Discourse: Fragments ; · Fragments and citations; · "[C]ontrolled accident" ("An Almost Obsessive Relation to Writing Instruments" 182) and the text's other structural and organizational features; · Barthes's use of Goethe's Werther; · "[T]he history of tears," "a scenography of waiting," and other extrapolations from the text (180, 37); · Relationships between this text and other works by Barthes, especially from the 1970s; · Barthes's (post)structuralist discussions of substitution, replication, and supplement; · Translation and differences between the French and English versions of the text; · Autotheory and other experimental, creative-critical practices inspired by Barthes; · (Loving) parodies of A Lover's Discourse ; · Anachronism in A Lover's Discourse both at the point of publication and now. As much as we trust that this conference will generate exciting new art and scholarship, we also hope to foster a substantial exchange of ideas and perspectives among all participants as well as personal interaction among scheduled presentations. Therefore, conference panels will be scheduled sequentially rather than concurrently so that all participants will be able to attend all panels, and we strongly encourage participants to stay for the duration of the conference. We believe that much good work will come from the conference, and we hope to assemble a collection of that work in the months following the conference in order to share it with the widest possible audience. Kicking off the conference will be a keynote address by Tufts professor John Lurz, author of The Barthes Fantastic: Literature, Criticism, and the Practice of Language . Please submit proposals of 350-500 words by email to Becky McLaughlin (email address: bmclaugh@southalabama.edu) and Eric Daffron (email address: edaffron@ramapo.edu) or by snail mail to Becky McLaughlin, Department of English, HUMB 240, University of South Alabama, Mobile, AL 36688. Due date: January 15, 2027.

items.title: Black Is...Black Is: Story as Construction and Celebration of Identity
items.location: Howard University · The Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association at Howard University
items.excerpt: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities an...
items.fullDescription: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities and identifications, and it cuts against the second half of his title, which suggests Blackness in terms of negation, evasion, and minimization. His articulation becomes not just an evocation of Black identifications but a creation of what a Black identity can be. Riggs continues a conversation with Ralph Ellison, Ama Ata Aidoo, Toni Morrison, Stuart Hall, and centuries of international Black thought. By doubling down on the "is" and considering contradictory, harmonious, and contrapuntal accounts of the many ways Blackness is and can be, the Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association hopes to join this dialogue with its March 25-26, 2027 conference. We invite papers that contemplate how storytelling produces and shapes Black identities as much as it narrates them, forming, revising, and improvising senses of self and community. This conference also does commemorative work. We are honoring the career of Dr. Jimisha Relerford, a graduate of our program and member of the Howard community who passed recently. Her dissertation broke critical ground in its study of Black women's satire. We thus encourage the submission of papers about Black satire, especially Black women's work in the genre. Writers such as Leone Ross, Danzy Senna, Fran Ross, and Zadie Smith, all of whom were discussed in Dr. Relerford's dissertation, use satire to comment on and transform notions of Blackness. We hope to continue Dr. Relerford's project by reflecting on how storytellers work within this genre to talk about identity. We additionally encourage studies of Afrofuturist and speculative Black texts in reference to our organization's namesake, a pillar in Afrofuturist study. In addition to recognizing the intellectual impacts of Drs. Relerford and Hampton, this conference serves as a milestone, marking the tenth conference our organization has hosted in honor of Black literary study. Given Black academia and HBCUs's influence on identity and storytelling around it, we also welcome papers pondering scholarly impacts on identity as seen in criticism, productions, and protest. We additionally invite papers in the following areas that intersect with identity and identification study in story: African Studies African-American Studies Caribbean Studies Disability Studies Ecocriticism and Ecopoetics Diaspora, Ethnicity, and Migration Studies Food Studies Hip Hop Humor Literary History Protest and Rhetoric Queer Studies Television and Film Theater and Performance To submit a paper or panel to our conference, please email an abstract of 250-300 words to gesasecretary@gmail.com no later than January 15, 2027. In your email include your name, affiliation, contact information, and a brief biographical blurb.

items.fullDescription: The Negative Journal is Calling for Papers for its third issue, co-edited by Dr Julie Reshe (editor-in-chief) and Dr Aaron Aquilina (guest editor). This is a general call for papers that also invites a special cluster on queer negativity. Call for Papers: General Issue There are many names for negativity: pessimism, nihilism, antinatalism, misanthropy, cynicism… sometimes absurdism, solipsism, or even mysticism, in certain senses. Some academic pursuit that teases out unique nuances among these terms would be - as are all pursuits - worthless. But expanding and conjoining these terms with more common parlance (depression, apathy, disappointment, suffering, meaninglessness) allows us, at bare minimum, to sketch our existence in a manner that makes legible and listens to these negative experiences rather than seeking to extinguish them through the fictions of therapy, companionship, hope, or love. This is not about being suicidal, at least not wholly. In the words of E.M. Cioran, '[w]e do not rush toward death, we flee the catastrophe of birth, […] source of every infirmity, every disaster' (The Trouble with Being Born). That place of non-being preceding our existence continues to haunt us throughout life, if we are unhappy enough to be attuned to it. Life is revealed, then, as 'death lived in postponement', and the void within makes of us the living dead, the being-not-being (Aaron Aquilina, The Ontology of Death). With these last remarks, and despite the proliferation of negativity's designations, one can quickly see how language begins to falter and fall into incomprehensibility; and perhaps not having the words for negativity is the most articulate anyone can be. Our horrified muteness is not merely some contemporary resignation in the face of 'global climate change, natural disasters, the energy crisis, and the progressive extinction of species world-wide' (Eugene Thacker, In the Dust of this Planet). Suffering has always been here, whether it is our own human condition or the pelicans' choking on plastic bottle caps. Depression, taken as a mode of (non-)being rather than reduced to a treatable illness, thus 'becomes a mode of knowing, a way of perceiving, of being touched and wounded by the world's wounds' (Julie Reshe, Negative Essays). This more-than-individual suffering only continues to manifest the negativity that thought acknowledges as its burden, arguably realised continually throughout history (Seneca and P.W. Zapffe come to mind). In light of this, the Negative Journal calls for papers that address negativity rather than pave the way for some illusory emancipation. Contributions might extend the thought of philosophical pessimists, inhabit the despair evident in literature and art, explore modes of non-being and un-becoming, or locate negativity in apophatic spaces beyond philosophy, psychoanalysis, and language. Work that interrogates negativity's limits, exclusions, political uses, and uneven distribution-as in Afro-pessimism or as per J. Logan Smilges's Crip Negativity-is equally welcome. The Negative Journal aims to provide a locus for these discussions, which are all too often deemed unspeakable. Special Cluster - Queer Negativity Additionally, this issue of the Negative Journal invites contributions towards a special cluster on queer negativity. The association of queerness with the death drive-that core negativity-is by now well established. Thinking through the consequences of this association in tandem with BAEDAN's anonymous editors, we come to realise that 'queer negativity […] means nothing less than the destruction of the civilized world' and its quiescent citizens. Queerness is figured, here, as a deadly anti-politics of the social and psychic alike, a void at the heart of it all. This act of connective thinking, however, is far from complete; indeed, it is even more urgent while late capitalism's assimilationist politics squeeze us harder than ever until we fit into 'intelligibility's mandate and the correlative economy that regulates what is ''legitimate and recognizable"' (Lee Edelman, No Future). Queers are encouraged to ally with the proponents of life on pain of perishing. The vigilant questions at the heart of this special cluster, then, are as follows: what constitutes the intersections of living queer and living death? How do queerness and negativity collude outside the domain of neoliberal homonormativity and its optimistically organised selves? One way would be to foreground the irruptions of various modes of death, rendering superfluous any attempt at positivist meaning-making out of queer subjectivity (to some extent or other, thinkers such as Michel Foucault, Judith Butler, Jeffrey Weeks and José Esteban Muñoz are proponents of this). That is, understanding how one can not participate in the warm embrace of 'the cult of difference' (Leo Bersani, 'Is there a Gay Art?'). And with figuring death's thwarting of "meaning" and "progress", of "community" and "generations" and "futures", come inquiries of the temporal privileges denied to those who insist on emptiness, unfixability, and death in the now not later. The positive time of social order can so easily be read as "straight time", after all (cf. Elizabeth Freeman, J. Halberstam, and others). Standing aside from the space of the polis and the time of life, what remains? Queer inchoate subjects, inarticulate and traumatised by life, humiliated and always-othered (…but somehow, always there…). Maladapted monsters, really: at best defined by mutations and gendered chimerism, at worst by viruses and the failure to participate in some grand narrative of reproductive evolution. These broken figures may be glimpsed in the history or the arts: what of them? What kind of pessimistic queerness, living through all sorts of deaths, can be read in novels, films, and other art forms in ways that are congruent with shoring up one's despair at life? But instead, perhaps, one should just laugh, for that is another way of fundamentally pulling the rug out from under those who deny life's disaster. Whether we shake with mirth or sobs, queerness no more pushes us towards desiring annihilation than acknowledges death's constant unworking of the self and its bonds. And speaking of desire: when considering selfhood against those charlatans that promise to fill the void, how is the scale that weighs sex and relations of un/knowing tipped one way or the other (cf. Oliver Davis & Tim Dean)? Too often for comfort, '[t]ransgressing limits [of sexuality] is to do with a vague notion of inclusiveness rather than active contravention', an affirmation rather than negation (Jonathan Dollimore, Sexual Dissidence). How, then, to wilfully pervert not just sexual practices but the tyrannical myth of happiness, which seeks to suffocate both negativity and queerness? In the end, more questions quibble in the corner: is queerness merely a layer on top of being that is always suffering? Or is it the case that, if queerness is another modulation of pessimist negativity, it is queerness itself that hurts? Submission Abstracts of no longer than 300 words (along with brief biographical notes) should be sent to julie.reshe@gmail.com and aaron.aquilina@um.edu.mt by 15th January, 2027. Submission emails should be headed by 'Negative Journal Issue 3 Submission' or 'Negative Journal Issue 3 - Queer Negativity'. Accepted papers extending the thoughts of this Call should be no longer than 4000 words, and less conventional and/or creative-critical forms are encouraged. Full pieces will be expected no later than by 1st June, 2027. items.fullDescription: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, frames are negotiated, shifted, and sometimes shattered in the movement between languages and cultures. They are the selective filters that highlight certain elements while relegating others to the background, the conceptual structures that allow us to categorize, interpret, and communicate complex realities.

items.fullDescription: (Re)Generation of the Nonhuman: Nature and Text in Dialogue The last decade has seen a surge in interdisciplinary scholarship, exploring the nonhuman in a broad range of critical perspectives. Whether through Glenworth et al (2024)'s conservationist prism which contextualizes 'Rewilding' as a way of restoring 'non-human autonomy'; or perhaps, through Bram Büscher (2021)'s capitalist reflections on nature's alienation and entanglement, both of which are recent approaches that seek to champion the cause of 'decentering the human in favor of a concern for the nonhuman' (Grusin, 2015: 1), we see a growing pace of intersectionality within which nature and literature are brazenly intertwined. Often suggested as a repressed generation of ecological beings, either of subaltern considerations or anthropomorphic (de)constructions, the nonhuman, whether plants, animals, or ecosystems, has continued to fit the bill for a contemporary kind of critical and textual narrative that urgently needs to undergo transformation through a process of generation, regeneration or auto-generation, after decades of being consistently synonymous with the image of depletive degeneration. David Abram (1996:22-23) describes the geographical space of this non-human depletion of nature as a biosphere of 'nonregenerative' decline, which in his views, has resulted in a variation of problems for humans: epidemics (including immune diseases and cancers) or perhaps, pandemics like the 2019 COVID which postdates Abram's study; or mental disorders. In the face of today's climate change and biodiversity loss, this collection proposes a constructive way of exploring literature's capacity to both reflect (on) the devastation of the natural world and, more importantly, provide imaginative models for its regeneration. Drawing on ecocritical theory, environmental humanities, animal studies, posthumanism, and new materialism, this collection invites papers that trace how literary texts can challenge anthropocentric templates, (re)imagining a textual world in which the nonhuman is seen as an active element with agency, living autonomously or forging a reciprocal connection with the human world. Scholars in French and Francophone Studies are invited to submit abstracts for a Bloomsbury critical collection exploring the relationship between literature and the nonhuman through interdisciplinary perspectives. Early and mid-career scholars are especially encouraged to submit. Authors must have a PhD. Papers can engage with, but are not limited to, the following themes: Ecocriticism (this includes, but are not limited to, a combination of ecocritical theories with other theories with the use of the prefix 'eco', e.g., ecofeminism, ecophenomenology, ecopoetics, ecocultural identities, ecoqueer, etc) Environmental Humanities Geocriticism Green Negritude Studies Green Cultural Studies Deep Ecology Dark Ecology Collapsology Spiralism Speciesism Blue Humanities Landscape Ecology Material ecocriticism Soundscape studies Animal Studies Race and Species Critical Plant Studies Multispecies Studies Indigenous Ecologies Black Ecologies Anthropocene Plantationocene Nonhuman Metamorphosis Afro-Caribbean Cosmologies Archipelagic Studies Environmental Aesthetics Ecological Kinship Créolisation and Ecological Relations Nonhuman Temporalities Decolonial Ecologies Environmental Justice Ecological Memory Please send proposals of 250-300 words and a 150 word biography to Israel Eweka at isreweka2019@outlook.com and Savannah DiGregorio at savannah.digregorio@asu.edu by January 25th, 2027. Notifications of acceptance will be sent by the end of February 2027. If accepted, full chapter drafts of approximately 6,000-8,000 words, including notes, will be due by July 5th, 2027.

items.fullDescription: Aviation has long captured the cultural imagination as a symbol of freedom, technological progress, and global connectivity. Yet it has also provided the backdrop for stories of crime, transgression, mystery, and fear. From hijackings and sabotage to smuggling, cybercrime, and high-profile investigations, aviation crime has inspired enduring narratives across popular culture, shaping public perceptions of safety, risk, and justice. This symposium invites scholars, practitioners, researchers, writers, and creators to explore aviation crime as both a lived reality and a cultural phenomenon. We welcome contributions examining the representation and interpretation of aviation crime in popular culture, including film, television, literature, digital media, journalism, true crime, gaming, and public memory. Bringing together diverse perspectives, the symposium seeks to examine how aviation crime is represented, experienced, remembered, and imagined. We welcome papers from researchers across the academic spectrum and encourage papers from postgraduate researchers and early career researchers. Topics can include, but are not limited to: • From headlines to Hollywood-Aviation Crime in Film, Television and Popular Media • Who is DB Cooper?-Folklore, Myth and Unsolved Mysteries • The Investigation continues-Journalism, True Crime and Public Memory • Picture Perfect Crime-Art, Illustration and Visual Culture • Paperbacks in the Seat Pocket-Fiction, Crime Writing and Literary Culture • To be continued…-Comics, Graphic Novels and Popular Print • If You See Something, Say Something-Security, Surveillance and Risk • Going Viral-Digital Media, Social Networks and Online Communities • Surely, you can't be serious?-Humour, Parody and Camp • Crime at 30,000ft-New Directions in Aviation Crime Studies • Flygirl, Femme Fatale, Fugitive-Women in aviation crime fiction and film To submit - please visit our portal to submit your 200-word abstract by 28 February 2027: Submission portal : https://unesurveys.au1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_8jjzaWnS732QsFE To register (free) : https://unesurveys.au1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_7TGWUYZidtlxVLU Please email queries to: info@aviationcultures.org

items.fullDescription: Introduction: I teach composition to both undergraduate upperclassmen and first-year graduate students at my university. In both these classes, I have found the curricular material available to me lacking in a couple of ways: either it's outdated or it's intended for doctoral-level readers who already have prior knowledge and a shared vocabulary. That makes reading for these classes in any meaningful way prohibitively difficult for many students. The threshold concepts that many of us who have taught writing for awhile share remain barriers for less experienced students or entry-level teachers. This collection will help those teachers who don't yet have tons of experience in the classroom or with doctoral-level research in the field. It bridges that gap. As editor, I want students or early-career teachers who access this collection to feel more confident in being well-informed about disciplinary conversations and better prepared to apply the real-world knowledge of more experienced teachers in their own classrooms. They should have a resource that doesn't require hours of wading through eye-crossing disciplinary jargon. This collection will use plain, easy-to-understand language. Objective: In short, purposeful chapters, this collection will help new and future teachers of writing better understand terminology or concepts in a way that fosters deep learning for themselves and application in their future classrooms. This book is, primarily, borne out of a need for a more context-appropriate textbook in an undergraduate and a master's-level introduction to composition studies course. Audience: The audience for this collection is upper-level undergraduate students and first-year graduate students just beginning to conceptualize what it means to teach writing at the high school or college level. In addition, this collection could be useful for teachers in other disciplines looking for clarification in writing pedagogy approaches outside their experience or instructional librarians tasked with supporting writing curriculum. Proposal submission procedure: Please complete and submit this form. Important Dates: Priority proposal submission deadline: December 1, 2026 Final proposal submission deadline: March 1, 2027 Submissions due end of 2027 Revisions due summer 2028 Early 2029 publication goal Send questions to: Dr. Jill Parrott, Professor of English Eastern Kentucky University jill.parrott@eku.edu Publishing info: Telling Teaching Writing is an open educational resource (OER) published by EKU Libraries housed in Manifold, a resource for open publishing supported by The Open Education Network (OEN). For more information about the requirements, benefits, and drawbacks for OERs, please read the Unesco statement on Open Educational Resources. This collection will exhibit the values of accessibility, equity, and inclusivity that open resources allow. Limited use of AI tools is acceptable for non-substantive purposes, such as proofreading, grammar correction, or general clarity improvements, provided that these tools do not generate new ideas, arguments, or original phrasing. Authors remain fully responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and originality of their submissions. By submitting a proposal, contributors affirm that their work will comply with this policy.
