items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS AND PRESENTATIONS AI AND THE IMAGINATION April 20-23, 2027 Oral Roberts University | Tulsa, Oklahoma, USA Proposal deadline: March 5, 2027 Rolling review; applicants will normally receive a decision within two weeks. In-person presentations only. Featuring Orson Scott Card, award-winning author of Ender's Game and Speaker for the Dead, with keynote speakers Pat Gelsinger, Joan Slonczewski, and Ben John. ABOUT THE CONFERENCE Oral Roberts University invites proposals for AI and the Imagination from participants across disciplines and professions. We welcome research, critical reflection, creative work, and practical applications. Students, faculty, researchers, educators, industry professionals, practitioners, faith leaders, writers, and artists are encouraged to contribute. Artificial intelligence is reshaping how we learn, work, create, and understand ourselves. The conference brings together conversations that too often occur separately, offering an opportunity to share ideas and experiences, question assumptions, and consider how our choices today will shape the years ahead. Interdisciplinary contributions are particularly encouraged. CONFERENCE TRACKS AI and the Imagination How have we imagined artificial intelligence, and how is artificial intelligence changing imagination itself? This signature track welcomes work involving science fiction, fantasy, film, literature, art, storytelling, speculative futures, AI-assisted creativity, and the ways imaginative works can help us understand possible technological futures. AI, Theology, and Ethics What theological, philosophical, and ethical questions arise from increasingly capable artificial intelligence? This track welcomes work on Christian theology and AI, ethics, human dignity, personhood, moral agency, wisdom, responsibility, vocation, technology and faith, and related philosophical or religious questions. AI, Human Agency, and Formation How does AI change what it means to think, choose, act, develop, and become? This track explores human agency in an age of increasingly capable AI, including cognitive and agency offloading, judgment and decision-making, autonomy, dependence, human-AI relationships, meaning, purpose, identity, formation, and human flourishing. AI and Teaching and Learning How is AI changing education and the work of teaching and learning? Topics may include pedagogy, assessment, academic integrity, AI literacy and fluency, faculty development, student learning, educational technology, curriculum design, personalized learning, and emerging models of education. AI, Society, and the Human Future What does widespread AI mean for individuals, communities, institutions, and society? Topics may include work, economics, culture, politics, law, relationships, inequality, democracy, social institutions, public policy, and the broader consequences of AI for the human future. AI, Leadership, Strategy, and Governance How should leaders make decisions in an AI-rich environment? This track welcomes work addressing leadership, organizational strategy, institutional transformation, governance, policy, risk, workforce development, and responsible AI adoption. AI, Research, Discovery, and Innovation How is AI transforming the process of discovery and the creation of new knowledge? This track includes AI-enabled research, interdisciplinary research methods, scientific discovery, innovation, entrepreneurship, and emerging approaches to scholarship and creative inquiry. SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Please include: • Presentation title • A 250-500-word abstract outlining the topic, approach, and main contribution of the proposed presentation • Preferred conference track • Presenter name(s) and institutional or professional affiliation, if applicable • Contact email(s) • Whether you plan to read a paper or give a presentation using slides A full paper or slide deck is not required at the proposal stage. Email proposals by March 5, 2027, to either conference co-organizer: Dr. Andrew Lang Dean, College of Science and Engineering Senior Professor of Mathematics Oral Roberts University alang@oru.edu Dr. Mark Hall Dean, J.D. McKean Library Senior Professor of English Oral Roberts University mhall@oru.edu Proposals will be reviewed as they are received. Early submissions are encouraged. PRESENTATION FORMAT All presentations will be delivered in person. Standard sessions allow 15 minutes for presentation followed by 5 minutes for questions and discussion. Accepted abstracts will be included in the online conference program. The conference will not publish formal proceedings or full papers. REGISTRATION Registration is required for all attendees, including accepted presenters. Please consult the conference website for registration information, hotel recommendations, schedule updates, and additional details. FEATURED SPEAKERS Orson Scott Card Award-winning author of Ender's Game and Speaker for the Dead. Pat Gelsinger Executive chair and head of technology at Gloo, general partner at Playground Global, and former CEO of Intel and VMware. His career spans more than 45 years in engineering and technology leadership. Joan Slonczewski, PhD Award-winning science fiction author and Professor of Biology at Kenyon College. Their novels include A Door into Ocean, Brain Plague, The Highest Frontier, and Minds in Transit. Their work explores evolution, biotechnology, artificial intelligence, and the future of intelligent life. items.fullDescription: "Creators of Gothic fiction have always been swift to take advantage of new media technologies", writes Joseph Campbell in Twenty-First Century Gothic, adding that "[t]he internet has proven to be no exception" (72). This special issue argues that horror storytelling on the internet - whether in the form of creepypasta (user-generated horror narratives that circulate online), collaborative digital storytelling universes, or multimodal digital narratives like podcasts, analog horror, and webseries - represents a vibrant contemporary evolution of the Gothic mode. Digital horror scholarship is a rich and rapidly expanding field, reflecting the increasing, and increasingly unsettling, centrality of the digital in our lives. Digital horror has been fruitfully interpreted through the lenses of digital culture and fan studies, as well as, recently, folklore and contemporary legend studies: Trevor Blank and Lynne McNeill's Slender Man Is Coming: Creepypasta and Contemporary Legends on the Internet (2018) positions Slender Man and other internet horror narratives as contemporary folklore, reading them in terms of community creation and ostensive practices, and Creepypasta, Digital Horror, and Legend Formation Across Interactive Media, a 2025 special issue of Contemporary Legend edited by Natalie Underberg Goode, picks up on the folkloric aspect of "'crowd-sourced' horror storytelling" and applies it to more recent digital horror phenomena (1). However, there is also a continuing critical tradition of reading digital horror as Gothic, from Isabella van Elferen's concept of the Cybergothic, which argues that "cyberspace is a spectral place haunted by the dualism of information and materiality" (2009, 99), to Jessica Balanzategui's delineation of the "digital Gothic" (2019) in the context of creepypasta narratives and Marc Olivier's concept of the "postdigital Gothic" (2021), which "calls attention to hidden architecture undergirding the virtual […] a vault of manuscripts buried beneath familiar interfaces" (323). Most recently, the 2026 International Gothic Association conference, Gothic Selves/Artificial Others, turned its attention to the Gothic aspects of AI technology, exploring "the intersections of Gothic literature, culture, and theory with artificial intelligence, automated creativity, and posthuman forms of subjectivity". Taken together, these approaches suggest the need to ask not simply how horror operates in digital media, but what happens when the distinctive structures, anxieties, and modes of participation of digital culture are understood through the Gothic. This special issue, then, foregrounds the specifically Gothic dimensions of digital horror, positioning this form of participatory, networked storytelling within a long Gothic tradition that extends from the 18th century to the present day. The volume explores how digital folklore reworks longstanding Gothic anxieties in contemporary modes, translating familiar structures of Gothic space, monstrosity, and uncertainty into the networked environment: the Backrooms, for instance, transpose the labyrinthine entrapment of the Gothic castle into vast, uncanny digital spaces, while internet-born monsters such as those catalogued by Line Henriksen in "A Short Bestiary of Creatures from the Web" (2013) emerge through processes of circulation, accumulation, and collective invention. The classic Gothic epistolary format is reimagined in forums like r/Nosleep (a subreddit for telling scary stories that purport to be true), wiki-style collaborative databases like the SCP Foundation, and found-footage web series, forms that invite audiences to participate in the reconstruction of events whose status as fictional or factual remains uncertain. This special issue asks how these narratives articulate contemporary anxieties around technological alienation, surveillance, epistemic uncertainty, unstable authorship, and the increasingly porous boundaries between reality and fiction. We welcome interdisciplinary contributions that explore digital horror through Gothic perspectives. Possible themes might include: - Digital horror folklore as Gothic storytelling - Nostalgia, remediation, materiality, lost media - Analog horror - Digital horror as epistolary Gothic - Alternate Reality Games and the boundaries between the screen and the world - AI horror, deepfakes, and algorithmic horror - Surveillance horror - Horror podcasts as Gothic storytelling - Digital hoaxes and curses - Dead media and the dead internet - Collaborative and crowdsourced storytelling - The postdigital Gothic and the digital as Gothic infrastructure Please submit proposals of ca. 500 words and brief biographies for consideration to both Elena Romea (University Carlos III of Madrid)) eromea@hum.uc3m.es and Erika Kvistad (University of South-Eastern Norway) erika.kvistad@usn.no by 1 March 2027 (include 'Gothic Studies' in the header). Completed articles are expected to be between 5,000-7,000 words. References Balanzategui, Jessica. "Creepypasta, 'Candle Cove', and the digital gothic". Visual Culture, 18.2 (2019), 187-208. Blank, Trevor and Lynne McNeill (eds). Slender Man Is Coming: Creepypasta and Contemporary Legends on the Internet. Utah State University Press, 2018. Campbell, Joseph. "Gothic Digital Technologies". The Ashgate Research Companion to Paranormal Cultures, eds. Olu Jenzen and Sally R. Munt. Ashgate, 2013. The International Gothic Association. Gothic Selves/Artificial Others. [Call for papers] Hull Gothic, 2025. https://hullgothic.wordpress.com/cfp/ Olivier, Marc. "Postdigital Gothic". items.fullDescription: Third Culture: Studies in Global Childhoods and Cosmopolitan Identities is a new peer-reviewed journal dedicated to the study of cultural and social issues related to complex cosmopolitan identities arising from mobile global childhoods which transcend conventional categories of migrancy and diaspora. Acknowledging Benedict Anderson's well-established idea that the nation is an imagined community, the specific focus of this journal is on the large and growing number of people whose identities are formed by the experience of having lived in three or more different nations during their childhoods. This is because there is already a substantial body of scholarly work on issues of migrancy, diaspora, and bicultural identities, so this journal was established to explore the experiences, perspectives, representations, and cultural productions of people whose mobile global childhoods have produced more complex cosmopolitan identities. Our first issue was published in May 2026, and for our second issue we are now inviting submissions which include: Scholarly articles based on original research in the arts (particularly literature) and/or the social sciences Book reviews Autobiographical narratives Original pieces of creative writing Please see the submission guidelines on the journal website: https://journals.sta.uwi.edu/ojs/index.php/tc/about/submissions Deadline: March 31, 2027 Editorial contact: thirdculturejournal@gmail.com
